definitions.definition: The limit that separates the caregiver's role from personal, social, financial or intimate involvement with a client.
Improper use of a client's money, property or person for another's gain.

procedures: At hire, every worker receives this policy, signs the Code of Conduct acknowledgment, and completes ethics and confidentiality training.
Caregivers provide only services listed in the client's service plan (PC-02). Requests for extra tasks are referred to the supervising RN.
Caregivers must not accept gifts, tips, loans or bequests from a client or family. If a gift is offered, the caregiver politely declines and reports it to the supervisor the same day (CR-04).

Caregivers must not borrow from or lend money to a client, buy or sell anything to or from a client, sign or use a client's checks or cards, hold a client's PIN or keys, or use a client's property, car or phone for personal use.
Caregivers must not engage in personal relationships with a client, share personal social media contact, post about clients, or take photos of clients, except as the client's service plan authorizes.
Caregivers must keep client information confidential and discuss it only with the agency's staff who need it (CR-03).

Caregivers must use ISAS only from the client's phone or approved device (PC-08). A caregiver whose personal phone number matches the client's phone number in ISAS must tell the Administrator before the first visit so another verification method can be arranged.
Caregivers are never to be under the influence of alcohol or drugs, smoke in a client's home without permission, or bring visitors or children to the home.
Caregivers must tell the Scheduler before accepting work privately from a current agency client or a client's family, and they may not solicit clients for private work.
A caregiver who is a relative of, or has a close personal relationship with, a client must tell the Administrator so any conflict can be reviewed.
A client may reject any caregiver without giving a reason. The agency offers another caregiver without retaliation against the client or the caregiver.
Any worker who knows about a possible violation reports it to the Administrator or the RN right away. Reports of abuse or exploitation follow ENV-08 immediately.
The Administrator investigates conduct concerns within five business days, interviews the people involved, and documents findings.
Discipline can include retraining, written warning, suspension or termination. The Administrator documents it in the personnel file.

If conduct may be grounds for Board of Nursing action, the Administrator reports it immediately to the Board of Nursing and OHCQ (COMAR 10.07.05.10). Substantiated abuse or exploitation is reported to the proper authorities (ENV-08).
The agency never retaliates against a worker or client for good-faith reporting.

responsibilities.duty: Enforces the Code of Conduct, investigates violations, imposes discipline and makes required reports.
Reinforces boundaries during supervisory visits and reports conduct concerns.
Follows the Code of Conduct and reports violations.
Offers a replacement caregiver when a client rejects a caregiver.

documentation: Signed Code of Conduct acknowledgment
Ethics and confidentiality training record
Conduct investigation notes and discipline records
Gift declined/reported log
Reports to the Board of Nursing, OHCQ or protective services

policies.title: Independent Contractors, Contractual Employees and Subcontract Agencies
policies.applies_to: Independent contractors, contractual employees and any agency that supplies personnel to [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To ensure workers supplied through contracts meet the same standards as employees, that subcontract relationships are disclosed to clients, and that worker classification is reviewed correctly.
policies.policy: Independent contractors and contractual employees who care for [AGENCY NAME] clients must meet the same screening, training and health requirements as employees (PER-03, PER-05, PER-06). A subcontract agency must verify personnel information for the workers it supplies and give the agency evidence of that verification, as COMAR 10.07.05.10 requires. The agency discloses any subcontract relationship to clients before services start. The agency reviews the classification of aides as employees or contractors against the guidance for Health-General §19-4A-11 and the RSA-PCA Guidance Document, and the person who controls pay and employment practices submits the OHCQ online RSA Certification form, which is a condition of obtaining and keeping the license.

definitions.definition: A worker who provides services under a written agreement and who is not an employee, as determined by the classification review.
A worker supplied to the agency under a contract whose personnel records are kept by the supplier.
Another agency that supplies workers or services to [AGENCY NAME] under a written contract.

procedures: Before using any independent contractor, contractual employee or subcontract agency, the Administrator completes a classification review using the guidance for Health-General §19-4A-11 and the RSA-PCA Guidance Document, and documents the result.

The person who controls the agency's pay and employment practices, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], reads the RSA-PCA Guidance Document and submits the OHCQ online RSA Certification form. A copy of the confirmation is kept with the license file.
The Administrator reviews classification again at least annually and whenever a role, schedule or degree of agency control changes.
Every contract is in writing. It states the services, rates, qualifications, requirement to follow agency policies, insurance, confidentiality, and the agency's right to end the contract.

Each independent contractor completes the same pre-referral screening as an employee: criminal history check, license or certification verification, health screening including TB, references, employment history, I-9 and identity/eligibility, in-person interview, and skills assessment and demonstration (PER-03, PER-04, PER-05).
Each contractor completes orientation, competency evaluation and annual training under PER-06 before assignment. The records go in a contractor file kept in the business office.

For a subcontract agency, the contract requires the agency to verify and give [AGENCY NAME] written evidence that each worker meets the personnel requirements, before the worker's first assignment and when requested.
The Administrator reviews the evidence, keeps a copy, and does not allow any worker to be assigned until it is satisfactory. The Administrator may audit the subcontract agency's files on request.
Contractors and subcontract workers follow the service plan and report to the supervising RN. The agency remains responsible for client care and for RN supervision (ADM-10).
Before services start, the Intake Coordinator tells each client in writing that a subcontract relationship exists, names the subcontractor, and records the disclosure in the client's record (CR-06).
Clients may accept or reject any referred caregiver, including a contractor, without retaliation.
The Administrator checks contractors and subcontract workers against the exclusion lists and registries before assignment and monthly after that (PER-03).
Annual contractor performance reviews are part of QA (ADM-08). Concerns are investigated like employee concerns, and a contract is ended for noncompliance.
Contractor and subcontract agency records are kept at least six years after the contract ends (PER-07).

responsibilities.duty: Reviews classification, signs contracts, completes the RSA Certification and reviews subcontract evidence.
Supervises contractor and subcontract workers on the same basis as employees.
Discloses subcontract relationships to clients.
Verifies personnel information and gives written evidence to [AGENCY NAME].

documentation: Classification review
RSA Certification confirmation
Signed contracts
Contractor files with screening, health and training records
Subcontract agency verification evidence
Client subcontract disclosure
Annual review

policies.title: Provision of Home Health Care Services and Criteria for Determining Need for Skilled Services
policies.applies_to: Clinical staff, intake staff and caregivers; all clients served by [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To state how [AGENCY NAME] provides home health care services and how the RN decides whether a client needs skilled services, so that clients get the right care from the right person.
policies.policy: This policy meets COMAR 10.07.05.08B(1)(c)(i) — Patient Care: Provision of home health care services and criteria for determining the need for skilled services (Application pp. 5–6). [AGENCY NAME] is a Residential Service Agency that provides home health aide and personal care services to unrelated sick or disabled persons in their homes. The agency provides skilled nursing only if it is listed on the agency's OHCQ license. The RN uses the written criteria in this policy to decide whether a client has a skilled need, at assessment and whenever the client's condition changes. When a skilled need is identified, the RN assesses the client within 48 hours, or within 7 calendar days if the RN documents that the 48-hour assessment is unnecessary. The RN then refers the client, coordinates care with another provider, or delivers the care if the agency is licensed to do so. A client who declines recommended skilled care signs a waiver after a documented risk/benefit discussion. A non-certified caregiver may be assigned only as COMAR 10.07.05.10 allows, and a certified caregiver is required where the client needs one for ADLs or medication administration.

definitions.definition: Services provided in the home to a sick or disabled person, as defined in COMAR 10.07.05.02.
A service that requires the judgment, knowledge and skill of a licensed nurse or other licensed professional.
An agency that employs or contracts workers to provide at least one home health care service to an unrelated sick or disabled person at home.
Activities of daily living, such as bathing, dressing, toileting, transferring, mobility and eating.
A caregiver who holds the certification required by COMAR 10.07.05 for care that requires it.

procedures: The Intake Coordinator records the client's requested services at first contact and checks that each requested service is within the agency's license and scope (ADM-02, ADM-05).
The agency does not accept a client whose needs cannot be met within its license. The Intake Coordinator refers the person to another provider and documents the referral (ADM-06).
The RN assesses each new client who needs skilled services and ADL help, as COMAR 10.07.05.12 requires, in the home before services start unless an exception applies and is documented.

At assessment the RN applies the Skilled Need Criteria and records the result on the Skilled Need Determination form. A skilled need is present if any of these exists: (a) a condition requiring nursing assessment or judgment, such as unstable vital signs or changing symptoms; (b) wound, pressure injury or skin care beyond basic hygiene; (c) injections, IV, enteral or parenteral feeding, catheter, ostomy, tracheostomy, oxygen or other nursing procedures; (d) medication administration, or complex medication management; (e) a new diagnosis, recent hospitalization or recent surgery; (f) teaching of a client or family that requires a nurse; or (g) any care a physician has ordered to be done by a licensed nurse.
The RN reapplies the criteria whenever the client's condition changes significantly, a caregiver reports a concern, the client or representative asks, a hospitalization ends, and at least annually.

When a skilled need is identified, the RN completes an assessment within 48 hours. If the RN documents that a 48-hour assessment is unnecessary, the assessment is completed within 7 calendar days, and the RN records the reason.

The RN then does one of the following and documents it: (a) refers the client to a licensed provider such as a home health agency or the client's physician; (b) coordinates the care with the other provider and defines each provider's role (ADM-03); or (c) provides the skilled care through agency nursing staff if skilled nursing is listed on the OHCQ license.
If the agency is not licensed for the skilled service, no agency staff perform it. The RN tells the client or representative and the Intake Coordinator what other providers may be available.
The RN notifies the client's physician or other provider of the assessment findings when appropriate and documents the communication.

The RN determines whether the client needs a certified caregiver. A non-certified caregiver may be assigned only if the client needs no ADL help, needs ADL help with no predictable adverse health consequences in the supervising nurse's judgment, or signs a waiver of skilled services (IC-03).

A certified caregiver is assigned whenever the client needs one for ADLs or for medication administration. Medication administration follows PC-03 and requires licensed or certified staff and physician orders.

If the client or representative declines recommended skilled care or a certified caregiver, the RN holds a documented risk/benefit discussion, explains alternatives, and the client signs and dates the waiver. A copy goes in the record (IC-03).
The RN builds the plan of care to reflect the skilled determination, the services, who provides them, when and how often, goals and safety measures (PC-02).
The RN updates the skilled need determination when plan changes occur, and records the date and reason.
The RN reports to the Administrator any client whose skilled needs exceed what the agency can safely provide. Discharge or transfer follows PC-10.
The Director of Nursing audits a sample of determinations quarterly as part of QA (ADM-08), and retrains RNs when the criteria are not applied correctly.

responsibilities.duty: Applies the criteria, completes timely assessments, decides on referral, coordination or delivery, and conducts the waiver discussion.
Maintains the criteria, audits determinations and ensures RN competence.
Screens requests against the license and scope and arranges referrals.
Ensures the agency provides only services listed on its license.
Reports changes in condition to the RN right away and does not perform skilled tasks.

documentation: Skilled Need Determination form
RN assessment with date and time
Documentation of 7-day exception reason when used
Referral and coordination notes
Signed waiver of skilled services with risk/benefit note
Plan of care
QA audit results

policies.title: Service Plan (Plan of Care/Plan of Service) and Plan Updates
policies.applies_to: All clients; RN Supervisor, Administrator, scheduler, caregivers; Medicaid CFC/CPAS participants and private-pay clients
policies.purpose: To make sure every client has a written plan of care (for Medicaid participants, a plan of service) that is based on an RN assessment, states what will be done and by whom, directs the participant's own role, and is reassessed and updated on time. For Medicaid participants, the plan keeps services within what the Department has authorized.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides services only under a written plan. An RN assesses each new client who needs skilled services or help with activities of daily living (ADLs), helps develop the plan and assigns staff. The plan states the services to be provided, when and how often, who provides them and how, long-range and short-range goals, and safety measures. For Medicaid CFC and CPAS participants, the Department-authorized plan of service names [AGENCY NAME] as the participant's chosen personal assistance agency, and the agency signs it. The caregiver schedule never exceeds the hours authorized in the plan of service. OLTSS standardized task times are used as the reference when hours for ADLs, IADLs and delegated nursing tasks are planned. The participant directs services: the participant or representative selects, trains, schedules, sets duties for and may dismiss the worker. The participant's representative may not be assigned as the worker. The RN reassesses at least annually, on client request, and on any significant change of condition. For Medicaid participants, services are not suspended, terminated, increased or reduced without Department authorization and consultation with the participant. This policy addresses the plan-of-care content and assessment-timing requirements of COMAR 10.07.05.12 and the Medicaid personal assistance conditions of COMAR 10.09.84.06.

definitions.definition: The agency's written plan for a client, developed with the RN, stating services, frequency, providers, goals and safety measures.

The Medicaid (CFC/CPAS) document that authorizes personal assistance hours and tasks for a participant and names the chosen agency. It is issued through the Department's process and signed by the agency.

A change in the client's health, function, cognition, safety or living situation that may require different services or hours, for example a hospitalization, a fall with injury, new confusion or loss of the primary support person.
The OLTSS standard times for assistance with ADLs, IADLs and delegated nursing tasks, used when assistance is planned and authorized.
The participant's right to take a significant role in selecting, training, scheduling, setting duties for and dismissing the worker.

procedures: The intake coordinator confirms, before the first visit, that a Medicaid referral includes an authorized plan of service that names [AGENCY NAME], the authorized hours and tasks, and the case manager or supports planner contact. This is recorded in the client record. Medicaid eligibility is verified at the start of each month of service (see ADM-13).

The RN Supervisor completes the in-person assessment before services start, except in limited situations allowed by COMAR 10.07.05.12. The assessment covers health status, ADL/IADL needs, cognition, home safety, medications, supports, preferences and risks.

If the client has a listed skilled need or a significant change of condition, the RN completes the assessment within 48 hours. If the RN documents that the 48-hour assessment is unnecessary, it is completed within 7 calendar days, and the RN's written reason is placed in the record.

The RN develops the plan of care with the client or representative. The plan states: each service; when and how often; who provides it (RN, CNA, CMT, or aide) and how; long-range and short-range goals; and safety measures. The RN also records whether a CNA is needed and which tasks, if any, are delegated.

For Medicaid participants, the RN compares the planned tasks and times to the authorized plan of service and the OLTSS standardized task times. Tasks or hours not authorized are not scheduled. The RN refers any gap between assessed need and authorized hours to the case manager or supports planner through PC-11.

The client or representative is invited to take part in the plan. The plan records the participant's preferences for worker selection, training, schedule and duties. The participant or representative signs the plan, and the client receives a copy.

The Administrator or designee signs the plan of service as the agency for Medicaid participants. Signing is not done until the RN has confirmed that the agency can staff the authorized hours, schedule and tasks.
The scheduler builds the caregiver schedule from the signed plan. Hours scheduled and recorded in ISAS may not exceed authorized hours (see PC-07 and PC-08).

The RN gives each assigned caregiver written worker instructions drawn from the plan before the first visit and documents that the caregiver received them. The RN reviews the instructions with the caregiver at the first supervisory visit.

Caregivers accept instruction about the plan of service from the participant or representative, the nurse monitor, a treating physician or nurse practitioner, or the Maryland Department of Health. A caregiver who receives such an instruction informs the RN the same day. Instructions that are unsafe, outside the caregiver's scope or outside authorized services are not carried out, and the RN is notified immediately.

The participant or representative may select, train, schedule, set duties for and dismiss the worker. The agency assists and does not retaliate. When a participant asks to dismiss or replace a worker, the scheduler arranges a replacement as soon as possible and documents the request. A participant's representative is never assigned as that participant's worker.

The RN reassesses and updates the plan: at least annually; at the client's request; and when there is a significant change of condition (see PC-09). Staff who observe a change report it to the RN within 24 hours, or immediately if urgent.

Any change to services for a Medicaid participant, including suspension, termination, or an increase or reduction in hours or tasks, is made only after Department authorization and consultation with the participant. The Administrator sends the transition plan to the case manager or supports planner and the participant when services end or change. A change that a private-pay client wants is documented as a plan revision with consent (see IC-01).

When a plan is revised, the RN documents the reason, updates the caregiver instructions, notifies the scheduler and assigned caregivers, and obtains the client's or representative's signature. The superseded plan is retained in the record.
The QA Committee audits a sample of plans each quarter for required elements, authorized-hours match, signatures, and reassessment dates (see ADM-08).

responsibilities.duty: Performs assessments, develops and updates the plan, determines delegation and CNA need, issues caregiver instructions, and documents reassessments.
Signs Medicaid plans of service for the agency, makes sure staffing supports the plan, and oversees compliance with authorization limits and Department notices.
Schedules only authorized hours consistent with the plan and arranges replacements as participants direct.
Follows the plan and worker instructions, accepts participant direction within scope, and reports changes in condition to the RN.
Takes part in the plan, directs services as allowed, and tells the agency of changes in needs.

documentation: RN assessment with date and time; the RN's written reason when the 48-hour assessment is extended to 7 calendar days
Signed plan of care or Department plan of service naming [AGENCY NAME], with the agency's signature
Written caregiver instructions and acknowledgment of receipt
Reassessment and plan revision records with reasons and signatures
Department authorization and transition-plan correspondence for Medicaid changes
Participant-direction preferences and worker change or dismissal requests

policies.title: Medication Assistance, Self-Administration Support and Administration of Drugs
policies.applies_to: All clients; RN Supervisor, CNAs, CMTs, aides and scheduler
policies.purpose: To state what [AGENCY NAME] staff may and may not do with medications, to protect clients from medication errors, and to meet the requirement that the agency have a policy on administration of drugs.
policies.policy: This policy meets COMAR 10.07.05.08B(1)(c)(ii) (Application p.6) — Patient Care: Administration of drugs. By default, aides assist only with self-administration of medications, and only after the client or representative gives signed informed consent. Administration of drugs, meaning that staff actually give the medication to the client, is performed only by licensed staff or by certified staff who are delegated by the RN. For Medicaid CFC/CPAS participants, a worker who administers medications must be a Certified Medication Technician (CMT), and a worker who performs other delegated nursing functions must also be a CNA. Administration requires a physician or other authorized prescriber order, and each medication, each error and each adverse reaction is documented. Medication errors and adverse reactions are reported to the RN immediately and recorded. RN on-site supervision is at least every 45 days when staff administer medications and at least every 3 months when staff assist with self-administration.

definitions.definition: Help given to a client who directs and takes his or her own medication, such as a reminder, retrieving or opening a container, or handing the client the medication the client has chosen to take. The client remains in control of the decision and the act.
Staff giving a medication to a client or choosing, preparing and giving it. It requires a licensed nurse or a CMT delegated under the RN's authority, and a prescriber order.
Certified Medication Technician: a certified staff member who may administer medications under RN delegation in Maryland.
Any wrong drug, dose, time, route or person, an omitted dose, or a dose given without an order.
An unexpected or harmful response to a medication, such as rash, breathing difficulty, severe drowsiness or confusion.

procedures: The RN Supervisor reviews medications at the initial assessment: the full list, prescribers, doses, schedule, allergies, who manages them now, and the client's ability to self-administer. The RN records the findings and the level of medication involvement in the plan of care.

The default plan is assistance with self-administration only. Before any aide assists, the RN discusses with the client or representative the purpose, alternatives, side effects and benefits, cost, and the right to withdraw. The client or representative signs and dates the consent (see IC-02), and a copy is placed in the record.

When assisting with self-administration, the aide may remind the client, bring the client's own labeled container, open the container, hand the client the medication the client selects, and observe that the client takes it. The aide may not decide the dose or time, change a dose, draw up or give injections, crush or mix medications unless the RN has instructed and delegated it, or give any medication the client has not chosen.

Administration is arranged only when the client cannot self-administer and the RN has confirmed a current prescriber order, a trained and certified staff member, and an authorized plan. For Medicaid participants, only a CMT (and a CNA for other delegated nursing functions) is assigned. The RN verifies certification before assignment.

The RN keeps a current written medication list and prescriber order for every medication staff administer. The RN contacts the prescriber if an order is unclear, incomplete or does not match the label, and does not allow administration until it is clarified.

Each time staff administer a medication, they document the medication name, dose, route, date and time, their name, the client's response and any refusal. For assistance with self-administration, they document that the reminder or help was given and whether the client took the medication.

A client may refuse any medication. The aide does not force or hide medication. The aide documents the refusal and notifies the RN the same day, or immediately if the medication is critical or the client seems unwell. The RN decides whether to contact the prescriber.

For any medication error or adverse reaction, the staff member stays with the client, calls 911 if the situation is an emergency, and notifies the RN immediately (24/7 on-call [PHONE]). The RN assesses, contacts the prescriber or poison control as needed, instructs the staff member, and documents the event.
The staff member completes an incident report the same day and the RN reviews it. The Administrator decides whether Department or OHCQ reporting applies under ENV-09 and REC-02.

The RN completes on-site supervision at least every 45 days for any client whose medications staff administer, and at least every 3 months for clients who receive assistance with self-administration. At each visit the RN reviews the medication documentation, observes practice, and checks for errors. Supervision is documented (see PC-05 and ADM-10).
Staff use only the client's own medications, stored where the client keeps them. Staff do not borrow, share, remove, buy or dispose of a client's medication, except as the RN instructs and documents.

If a client's ability changes so that assistance is no longer enough, the aide reports it to the RN within 24 hours. The RN reassesses, updates the plan with consent (see IC-01) and arranges a CMT or licensed nurse, or refers the client to another provider if the agency cannot meet the need.

Medication assistance and administration are included in orientation and annual training, with return demonstration for staff given delegated tasks (see PER-06). The QA Committee reviews errors, adverse reactions and documentation audits quarterly (see ADM-08).

responsibilities.duty: Assesses medication needs, obtains consent, delegates to CMTs, verifies orders, responds to errors and reactions, and supervises at the required intervals.
Administers only medications ordered by an authorized prescriber and documents each dose, refusal, error and reaction.
Assists only with self-administration after consent, never administers, and reports refusals, errors and reactions immediately.
Ensures only qualified staff are assigned and determines external reporting of medication events.

documentation: Medication list and prescriber orders
Signed informed consent for non-licensed assistance (IC-02)
Medication administration or assistance records
Refusal, error and adverse reaction records and incident reports
CMT and CNA certification verification
RN supervisory visit notes with dates

policies.title: Enteral and Parenteral Nutrition Procedures
policies.applies_to: All clients; intake staff, RN Supervisor, scheduler and caregivers
policies.purpose: To state that [AGENCY NAME] does not provide enteral or parenteral nutrition, to protect clients from care outside the agency's scope, and to describe what happens when a client needs it.
policies.policy: This policy meets COMAR 10.07.05.08B(1)(c)(iii) (Application p.6) — Patient Care: Enteral and parenteral nutrition procedures. [AGENCY NAME] does not provide enteral (tube) feeding or parenteral (IV) nutrition. Aides, CNAs and CMTs must not perform, set up, manage, flush, adjust or troubleshoot enteral or parenteral nutrition or related equipment. A client who needs this service is referred to a licensed provider that offers it, and the RN documents the referral. The agency does not accept a client whose care depends on these services unless another provider delivers them and the agency's own services are limited to tasks within its scope. The agency may add the service only after the RN writes the procedures, OHCQ is notified of the change in services under the RSA license, and this manual is revised and staff are trained.

definitions.definition: Nutrition delivered through a tube into the stomach or intestine, such as a G-tube or J-tube.
Nutrition or fluids delivered into a vein through an IV or central line (TPN or PPN).
A documented handoff of a client's need to a licensed provider that offers the service.

procedures: At intake, the intake coordinator asks every referral source and client whether the client uses or is expected to use a feeding tube, IV line, port or parenteral nutrition, and records the answer.
If the answer is yes, the intake coordinator refers the screening to the RN Supervisor before accepting the client (see ADM-05 and ADM-06).

The RN Supervisor assesses the client's needs, identifies who will provide the enteral or parenteral care, and decides whether [AGENCY NAME] can safely serve the client within its scope. If it cannot, the RN explains this to the client or representative.

If another licensed provider (for example a home infusion, home health or private duty nursing provider, or the client's family trained by that provider) delivers the nutrition, the RN documents who provides it and records in the plan of care that agency staff do not perform or manage it. The plan lists the tasks agency staff may do.

If no provider is in place, the RN refers the client to the physician, case manager or supports planner, or a licensed provider offering the service, gives the client or representative at least two options when available, and records the referral date, contact and outcome.

The RN gives caregivers written instructions that they must not touch, handle or adjust any tube, pump, line or formula, and that they may do only the permitted tasks listed in the plan, such as positioning, hygiene, and reporting.
A caregiver who is asked by anyone to perform enteral or parenteral care declines, explains that the agency does not provide it, and notifies the RN the same day.

A caregiver who notices a problem with a tube or line (dislodged tube, leaking, pain, redness, bleeding, fever, difficulty breathing, vomiting, coughing or choking) stops any activity involving the client's position or movement that may worsen it, calls 911 for any emergency, and notifies the RN immediately (see PC-09).
The RN assesses the situation, contacts the responsible provider or physician, documents the event, and completes an incident report when required (see ENV-09).

If a client's condition changes so that new enteral or parenteral nutrition begins during service, the RN reassesses within 48 hours (or within 7 calendar days if the RN documents that 48 hours is unnecessary) and updates the plan, or discharges following PC-10 if the agency cannot safely continue.

If the agency decides to offer this service, the Administrator may do so only after: the RN writes procedures and a training and competency plan; the governing authority approves; OHCQ is notified and any license update completed before service starts; the manual is revised (ADM-01, ADM-11); and staff competency is verified before assignment.
The QA Committee reviews referrals made under this policy and any incidents involving tubes or lines at least annually.

responsibilities.duty: Screens and assesses clients needing these services, documents referrals, and instructs caregivers on limits.
Screens for tube feeding or IV therapy at intake and escalates to the RN.
Does not perform enteral or parenteral care, reports problems to the RN, and calls 911 in emergencies.
Ensures the service is not provided without governing authority approval, OHCQ notification and manual revision.

documentation: Intake screening record
RN assessment and scope determination
Referral documentation with dates and outcome
Plan of care showing who provides nutrition and agency staff limits
Written caregiver instructions
Incident reports for tube or line events

policies.title: Frequency of Client Monitoring
policies.applies_to: All clients; RN Supervisor, scheduler, Administrator and caregivers
policies.purpose: To set how often [AGENCY NAME] monitors each client, including RN reassessments, RN on-site supervisory visits and cooperation with Medicaid nurse monitoring, so changes in condition and care quality problems are found early.
policies.policy: This policy meets COMAR 10.07.05.08B(1)(c)(iv) (Application p.6) — Patient Care: Frequency of client monitoring. The RN sets the monitoring schedule at the first assessment and records it in the plan of care. RN on-site supervision is at least every 45 days when staff administer medications, at least every 3 months when staff assist with self-administration of medications, and at least every 4 months otherwise, or more often when the RN decides. The RN reassesses at least annually, on client request, and on a significant change of condition. Medicaid nurse monitoring is separate from the agency's own supervision: the nurse monitor contacts the participant every 6 months and visits in person every 12 months, and agency staff cooperate fully. Each supervisory visit is documented.

definitions.definition: An RN visit to the client's home to observe care, review documentation, evaluate the client's condition and the caregiver's performance, and update the plan.
A full RN assessment of the client's condition and needs, done at least annually and on request or significant change.
The Medicaid-program nurse who monitors a participant's services under CFC. This is separate from the agency's RN.

procedures: At the initial assessment the RN Supervisor determines the client's medication involvement (none, assistance with self-administration, or staff administration) and sets the supervisory interval: 45 days, 3 months or 4 months. The interval and the next due date are written in the plan of care.

The RN sets a more frequent interval when risk warrants, for example high fall risk, cognitive impairment, a new or inexperienced caregiver, wound or skin concerns, recent hospitalization, a complaint or incident, or any client or family concern. The reason is documented.
The office coordinator enters every client's next supervisory visit date and annual reassessment date into the monitoring tracker at admission.
The coordinator gives the RN a due list at the start of each month and sends a reminder at least 10 days before each due date. The RN schedules the visit with the client or representative.

At each on-site visit the RN observes the caregiver providing care when possible, reviews the plan with the client, checks the home for safety, reviews medication records, assesses skin, mobility, nutrition and mood, asks about satisfaction and any concerns, and checks that the schedule and service delivery match the plan.

If medication involvement changes, the RN changes the interval at once and the next visit is set under the shorter interval. A client who moves to staff administration is seen within 45 days of the change or sooner.
The RN documents each supervisory visit the day it occurs with date, observations, findings, actions taken and any plan update. Plan changes are shared with the client, caregivers and scheduler.

The RN completes a reassessment at least annually, at the client's request, and within 48 hours of learning of a significant change in condition or a listed skilled need (within 7 calendar days if the RN documents the 48-hour assessment is unnecessary). See PC-02 and PC-09.

Between RN visits, caregivers report changes of condition to the RN within 24 hours, or immediately if urgent. The office contacts the client or representative at least monthly, including when collecting the monthly signature verifying services for Medicaid participants, and asks about care quality and changes.

If a visit cannot be completed because the client is unavailable or refuses entry, the RN documents each attempt, contacts the client or representative by phone, and reschedules within 7 calendar days. If the due date will pass, the RN tells the Administrator, who decides if further action is needed.

Any supervisory visit that is overdue is reported to the Administrator immediately. The Administrator confirms it is done within 7 days and records the reason for the delay. The delay is reviewed by QA.

Staff cooperate with the Medicaid nurse monitor, who contacts the participant every 6 months and visits in person every 12 months. The RN or office provides requested records, arranges access to the participant and caregivers, and acts on the nurse monitor's recommendations within the time the nurse monitor requests (see PC-11).

The office records each nurse monitor contact and follow-up. Nurse monitor findings are reviewed with the RN and added to the plan when they affect care. The agency's own RN supervision is not replaced or reduced by nurse monitor visits.
The QA Committee reports each quarter on the percentage of supervisory visits and reassessments completed on time. The goal is 100 percent (see ADM-08).

responsibilities.duty: Sets intervals, performs supervisory visits and reassessments, and documents each visit.
Maintains the monitoring tracker, issues due lists and reminders, and records nurse monitor contacts.
Reviews overdue visits, supports staffing for RN visits and ensures cooperation with nurse monitors.
Reports changes of condition promptly and takes part in supervisory observation.

documentation: Plan of care showing the supervisory interval and next due dates
Monitoring tracker and monthly due lists
RN supervisory visit and reassessment notes
Records of attempts to reach clients and reschedule
Nurse monitor contact and follow-up log
QA monitoring reports

policies.title: Training and Retraining of Clients and Family Members
policies.applies_to: All clients and their family members or representatives; RN Supervisor and caregivers who reinforce training
policies.purpose: To make sure clients and family members are taught what they need to know to take part safely in care, and that training is repeated when circumstances change.
policies.policy: This policy meets COMAR 10.07.05.08B(1)(c)(v) (Application p.6) — Patient Care: Training and retraining of clients or their family members, when indicated. The RN identifies training needs at assessment and at each supervisory visit, including safe transfers, use of equipment, self-administration of medications, infection precautions, and signs that should prompt a call to the agency. Training respects the client's rights to take part in the care plan, to refuse, and to make informed decisions. Teaching and teach-back are documented in the record. Training is repeated when the client's condition, equipment or caregivers change. Participants who direct their own workers are trained for that role.

definitions.definition: A method in which the learner explains or demonstrates what was taught so the RN can confirm understanding.
Repeat teaching because of a change in condition, equipment, caregivers or because the learner has not shown understanding.
Training that helps a Medicaid participant or representative select, train, schedule, set duties for and, if needed, dismiss a worker.

procedures: At the initial assessment, the RN Supervisor identifies what the client and family need to learn, based on the client's condition, home, equipment, medications and support network, and records the topics in the plan of care.

The RN identifies the right learner (client, family member or representative), the learner's ability, language, literacy and learning preferences, and arranges interpretation or translation when needed (see CR-05).

The RN teaches in the home using plain language and demonstrations. Typical topics are safe transfers and body mechanics, use and care of equipment such as walkers, lifts and commodes, fall prevention, skin care, hand hygiene and infection precautions, self-administration of medications and storage, emergency steps, and when to call the agency or 911.

For medication self-administration, the RN covers purpose, alternatives, side effects and benefits, cost, and the client's right to withdraw consent, consistent with IC-02 and the rights policy in CR-01.
The RN uses teach-back for each topic. If the learner cannot demonstrate understanding, the RN repeats the teaching, simplifies it or arranges another method, and records the result.
The RN gives written instructions suited to the learner's language and ability. The 24/7 telephone number [PHONE], and the supervisor's name and contact are included.
The RN documents each session in the record on the day it occurs: topic, learner, method, materials given, teach-back result, remaining needs and follow-up date.
If a client or family member declines training, the RN respects the decision, explains the risks and alternatives, documents the discussion, and adjusts the plan of care accordingly (see IC-01).

The RN retrains when the client's condition changes, new equipment is delivered, a new caregiver or family member takes over care, a mistake or near miss occurs, or the client asks. The RN checks understanding of earlier topics at every supervisory visit (see PC-05).

When a Medicaid participant or representative directs the worker, the RN or Administrator explains the participant's role in selecting, training, scheduling, setting duties for and dismissing the worker, the agency's responsibilities, and how to reach the agency for help. The participant is offered help in writing duties and in training the worker, and the explanation is recorded.

Caregivers reinforce the RN's teaching during visits and do not substitute their own instructions for clinical teaching. They tell the RN when the client or family appears confused, unsafe or in need of retraining.

The RN does not train family members to perform skilled tasks on behalf of the agency. When family members will perform tasks, the RN teaches what the plan allows and clarifies that they act as family members, not agency staff.
The QA Committee reviews a sample of records each quarter for documented training and teach-back (see ADM-08).

responsibilities.duty: Identifies needs, teaches, verifies understanding, retrains and documents each session.
Reinforces the RN's teaching and reports signs that retraining is needed.
Ensures materials, interpretation services and RN time are available.
Takes part in training and tells the agency when help is needed.

documentation: Training needs identified in the assessment and plan of care
Dated teaching notes with teach-back results
Copies of written instructions given
Documentation of refusal of training and risk discussion
Participant-direction explanation and training record
Interpreter or translation use

policies.title: Scheduling, Missed Visits and Continuity of Care
policies.applies_to: All clients; scheduler, RN Supervisor, Administrator and caregivers
policies.purpose: To make sure care is scheduled within authorized hours, that missed visits are handled quickly and safely, and that clients receive continuous care without unauthorized changes in service.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] schedules caregivers for no more than the hours authorized in the Medicaid plan of service or agreed in the private-pay service agreement, and delivers services consistent with the plan. When a visit is missed, the agency notifies the client, arranges a replacement, and notifies the RN if the client's health or safety is at risk. When one aide serves two Medicaid participants in the same home setting at the same time, the agency uses the shared-attendant codes (W5521 for CFC and W5528 for CPAS, $4.2597 per 15 minutes under PT 03-25) only if the plan of service authorizes shared attendant services. A daily rate applies above 12 hours per day (W5532, $329.84) only where authorized. Services for Medicaid participants are not suspended, terminated, increased or reduced without Department authorization and consultation with the participant. Clients may accept or reject any caregiver without retaliation.

definitions.definition: The hours and tasks approved in the Medicaid plan of service. The agency may schedule and bill no more than this.
A scheduled visit that does not occur at the scheduled time because the caregiver is absent, late beyond the agreed window, or the visit is not staffed.
One aide serving two participants at the same time under shared-attendant authorization, billed under W5521 (CFC) or W5528 (CPAS).
A qualified caregiver who covers a visit when the assigned caregiver cannot, with the client's agreement.

procedures: Before creating or changing a schedule, the scheduler checks the signed plan of service or service agreement for authorized hours, tasks, and any shared-attendant or daily-rate authorization, and confirms Medicaid eligibility has been verified for the current month (see ADM-13).

The scheduler matches caregivers to the client's needs, preferences, language, and location, and checks that the caregiver's qualifications and any delegated-task requirements are met (see PER-02). The caregiver's name and the care supervisor's name and contact are given to the client.

The scheduler enters the schedule so that weekly and daily hours do not exceed authorized hours. A request that would exceed the authorization is not scheduled, and the scheduler refers it to the RN Supervisor.
The scheduler records the participant's preferences about days, times and worker, and honors the participant's right to direct the schedule within the authorization.

A client or representative may refuse or ask to replace any caregiver at any time. The scheduler records the request, arranges a replacement promptly, and takes no retaliatory action. A participant's representative is never scheduled as that participant's worker.

A caregiver who cannot work a visit calls the office as soon as the problem is known, and when possible at least [2] hours before the visit. The scheduler logs the call and starts replacement at once.

The scheduler calls the client or representative immediately to say the visit is delayed or changed, tells them who will come and when, and records the call. The client may accept the replacement or reschedule within the authorized period.

If no replacement is available, the scheduler informs the client and the RN Supervisor right away. The RN decides whether the client's health or safety is at risk, for example missed medication assistance, toileting or transfer needs, living alone with cognitive impairment, and arranges an alternative: another caregiver, family or back-up contact, or referral for emergency help.

If a caregiver arrives and cannot get in or the client is not responding, the caregiver calls the client, then the emergency contact, then the office. The RN directs next steps. The caregiver calls 911 for any concern for the client's safety, and the incident is documented (see PC-09 and ENV-09).
Time worked is recorded only in the Department-approved telephonic timekeeping system (ISAS) (see PC-08). A replacement caregiver clocks in and out in the same way. Missed visits are not billed.

Services for a Medicaid participant are not suspended, terminated, increased or reduced by the agency without Department authorization and consultation with the participant. A client request for more or fewer hours or tasks is referred to the case manager or supports planner. If services must end or change, the Administrator follows PC-10 and sends the transition plan to the case manager or supports planner and the participant.

When one aide serves two Medicaid participants in the same setting, the scheduler confirms that both plans authorize shared attendant services, schedules and bills under W5521 (CFC) or W5528 (CPAS) as authorized, and the RN documents how both clients' needs are met. Shared care is not used when it would reduce either client's safety or authorized care.
Each week the scheduler reviews the previous week's missed and late visits and gives a log to the RN Supervisor. The log records the client, date, reason, replacement, notification and any harm.

Back-up coverage is maintained by having at least one other caregiver familiar with each client's plan, and the on-call RN available 24/7 at [PHONE] (see ADM-10). For clients with high-risk needs, the RN names a back-up in the plan.
The QA Committee reviews missed-visit rates, causes and trends each quarter, and the Administrator takes action on repeated problems (see ADM-08).

responsibilities.duty: Schedules within authorization, handles call-outs and replacements, notifies clients, and keeps the missed-visit log.
Assesses risk from missed visits, directs alternative care and sets back-up arrangements for high-risk clients.
Ensures adequate staffing, prevents unauthorized changes in service, and handles transition plans.
Reports inability to work promptly, uses ISAS correctly, and follows welfare-check steps.

documentation: Schedules and changes with authorization check
Missed-visit log with notifications and replacements
Client requests to change caregivers
Shared-attendant authorization and billing records
Department authorization and transition-plan correspondence
Incident reports for missed visits with harm or risk

policies.title: Electronic Visit Verification (ISAS) and Timekeeping
policies.applies_to: All aides, RNs and other staff who deliver Medicaid personal assistance (CFC, CPAS, Community Options); scheduler, billing staff, ISAS administrators and the Administrator
policies.purpose: To make sure every hour of Medicaid personal assistance is verified electronically at the time it is delivered, paid correctly, and supported by accurate records. This meets the federal electronic visit verification requirement (42 U.S.C. §1396b(l)), which Maryland satisfies through its telephonic timekeeping system, ISAS.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] uses the Department-approved telephonic timekeeping system (ISAS) to document time and submit claims for all Medicaid personal assistance. ISAS is the only way the agency bills this service. Aides clock in by phone at the start of each shift and clock out by phone at the end, from the participant's primary landline or from the participant's One-Time Password (OTP) device. An aide's own phone number must never match the participant's number. Aides may not clock in or out for someone else, and no one may create, alter or back-fill time to resemble a visit that did not occur. Time worked beyond the hours in the participant's plan of service is automatically reduced by ISAS and is not paid, so the agency schedules and monitors visits to stay within authorized hours. The agency is paid the lesser of its usual and customary charge to the general public or the Medicaid fee schedule rate, in 15-minute units for up to 12 hours per day and at the daily rate above 12 hours. Claims are submitted within 12 months of the date of service. ISAS portal access is limited to authorized agency staff; aides cannot log in to the portal. The missing-time limits and deadlines in this policy come from MDH's 2020 ISAS training. The Administrator confirms current rules with the ISAS Help Desk (1-855-463-5877) at least once each quarter and updates this policy when they change.

definitions.definition: The Maryland Department of Health's telephonic electronic visit verification and billing system used for Community First Choice, CPAS and Community Options personal assistance. ISAS generates the claims.
A One-Time Password device placed in a participant's home that generates a code used to verify the visit location when the participant has no usable primary landline.
A request to add or correct time in ISAS when an aide could not clock in or out correctly.
Portal user roles assigned to agency staff. Up to 5 administrative and 5 billing roles may be assigned per agency.
The ISAS workweek, which runs Thursday through Wednesday.

procedures: At intake, the Scheduler records the participant's primary landline number or confirms that an OTP device is in the home. The Scheduler confirms the verification method with the participant before the first visit and documents it in the client record.

Before the first shift, the Scheduler checks that the aide's personal phone number is not the same as the participant's verification number. If the numbers match, the Scheduler stops the assignment and corrects it before any visit.

During orientation (PER-06), the Administrator or designee trains each aide in clocking in and out by phone or OTP device. Training covers what to do if the system does not respond. The aide signs a statement acknowledging this policy.

The Administrator names ISAS portal users, with no more than 5 administrative and 5 billing roles. The Administrator keeps a log of who holds each role, the date assigned and the date removed. Access is removed on the day a user leaves or changes duties.
The aide clocks in by phone from the participant's landline or OTP device when the visit begins, and clocks out when it ends. The aide never clocks in before arriving or after leaving.

The Scheduler sets each aide's weekly schedule so that scheduled hours stay within the hours authorized in the participant's plan of service. Hours beyond the plan are not scheduled without documented Department authorization.

Each business day, the Billing Coordinator reviews ISAS for visits with no clock-in, no clock-out, a mismatched number or hours above plan. The Billing Coordinator calls the aide the same day to find out what happened.

If a visit was worked but the clock-in or clock-out failed, the Billing Coordinator checks the facts with the aide and participant and submits a missing-time request only for time actually worked. Per 2020 MDH training, the number of missing-time requests is limited to 4 per period and requests are due within 2 business days after month end. The Billing Coordinator tracks the count and the due date for every pay period.
The Billing Coordinator tracks time on the ISAS Thursday–Wednesday workweek and keeps a weekly list of unresolved exceptions, with the aide, date, reason and action taken.

The Administrator reviews the exception list weekly. An aide with repeated clocking errors receives retraining. Suspected falsification is handled under ADM-12 and may lead to discipline up to termination and referral to the proper authorities.

Before submitting any claim, the Billing Coordinator confirms that the service is in the plan of service, the visit was verified in ISAS, and the units do not exceed authorized hours. ISAS-generated claims are submitted within 12 months of the date of service. The agency aims to submit within [NUMBER OF DAYS] days of service.
Time over authorized plan hours that ISAS reduces is not billed to the participant or the Medicaid program. The Billing Coordinator documents any reduction and reports patterns to the Administrator.
Private-pay or non-ISAS visits are timed through the agency's own timekeeping system described in ADM-07. Time is never mixed between systems.
Aides are paid for all hours worked under PER-08. If ISAS does not pay for time the aide worked, the Administrator reviews the cause and the agency pays the aide for that time.

Each quarter, the Administrator calls the ISAS Help Desk (1-855-463-5877) to confirm the missing-time limit, deadlines, workweek and verification rules in this policy. The Administrator records the date, the staff person spoken to and any change, and revises this policy and trains staff within 30 days of a change.

responsibilities.duty: Owns this policy; assigns and removes ISAS portal roles; confirms current ISAS rules with the Help Desk; investigates suspected falsification.
Records each participant's verification method; prevents aide and participant numbers from matching; schedules within authorized hours.
Reviews ISAS exceptions daily; files missing-time requests on time; checks claims before submission; tracks the missing-time count and deadlines.
Clocks in and out from the participant's landline or OTP device at the true start and end of each visit; reports any problem the same day.
Reports observed discrepancies between care delivered and time recorded.

documentation: ISAS role assignment log
Participant verification method record (landline or OTP device)
Daily and weekly ISAS exception lists
Missing-time requests with the facts and dates submitted
Aide training and acknowledgment of this policy
Quarterly Help Desk confirmation log
Claim submission and reduction records

policies.title: Change in Client Condition and Emergencies in the Home
policies.applies_to: All caregivers, RNs, schedulers, on-call staff and the Administrator
policies.purpose: To make sure that a significant change in a client's condition, or an emergency in the home, gets a fast and safe response and a timely RN assessment. It also makes sure that advance directive information is honored and that every event is documented and reported.
policies.policy: Every caregiver is trained to recognize a significant change in a client's condition and to call the RN. This training is part of the minimum content required for in-home care. In an emergency, the caregiver calls 911 first, then the RN or on-call nurse, then the client's family or representative. The agency keeps a registered nurse reachable 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, who responds within 1 hour, and keeps a log of on-call calls. The RN assesses a client within 48 hours after a significant change in condition. If the RN documents that the 48-hour assessment is unnecessary, the assessment is done within 7 calendar days. Advance directive information in the client record is checked and honored. Incidents are reported under ENV-09, and suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation under ENV-08.

definitions.definition: A new or worsening sign, symptom, behavior or functional decline that differs from the client's usual state, or that could affect the client's safety or the services in the plan of care. Examples are a fall, new confusion, breathing difficulty, chest pain, new skin breakdown, refusal of food or fluids, a hospitalization, or a decline in the ability to do activities of daily living.

A situation that threatens life, safety or health and needs immediate help, such as unresponsiveness, difficulty breathing, severe bleeding, stroke or heart attack signs, a serious fall, fire, or a threat of violence.
The registered nurse designated to be reachable at all hours and to respond to calls within 1 hour.

procedures: During orientation, the RN trains each caregiver to recognize a significant change in condition and the situations that need RN referral. Training also covers the plan for contacting 911, the on-call number and CPR. The caregiver's competency is checked and recorded under PER-06.
Each client's plan of care lists the client's baseline condition, usual routine, and the signs the caregiver should report. The caregiver reviews it before the first visit.
In an emergency, the caregiver calls 911 first and gives the address, the client's condition and what has been done. The caregiver does not delay calling 911 to reach the agency.

The caregiver gives only the first aid and CPR in which the caregiver has been trained. The caregiver stays with the client, does not move an injured client unless there is immediate danger, and does not give medications that are not in the plan of care.

Before the emergency team arrives, the caregiver checks the client record or the home for an advance directive or other life-sustaining treatment order. The caregiver shows it to emergency responders and follows the agency's procedure under IC-04. The caregiver never makes the decision for the client.
After calling 911, the caregiver immediately calls the RN or on-call number at [PHONE], and then the client's family or representative. The caregiver notes the time of each call.

For a change in condition that is not an emergency, the caregiver reports it to the RN or on-call number as soon as it is noticed and before leaving the home. The caregiver does not wait for the next scheduled supervisory visit.

The on-call RN answers within 1 hour. The RN gets the facts, decides whether to send the client to emergency care, contact the physician or other provider, or increase monitoring, and gives the caregiver clear instructions. The RN logs each call with time, caller, client, concern and action in the on-call log.

The RN assesses the client within 48 hours of the report of a significant change. If the RN decides after talking with the caregiver that a 48-hour assessment is unnecessary, the RN records the reason in the record, and the assessment takes place within 7 calendar days.

After the assessment, the RN updates the plan of care under PC-02 and tells the caregiver, the client or representative and, as appropriate, the physician and the case manager or supports planner. A change to the recommended plan of care that the client declines is handled under IC-01.

The caregiver completes an incident or change-in-condition report on the day of the event and gives it to the RN. The RN submits incidents under ENV-09, and the Administrator makes any required reports under REC-02.
If the event raises a concern of abuse, neglect, self-neglect or exploitation, the caregiver or RN follows ENV-08 immediately.

The Administrator reviews each emergency and each significant change event within 7 days. This review looks at the response time, whether the policy was followed, and whether training or staffing needs to change. Results go to the Quality Assurance Committee under ADM-08.

responsibilities.duty: Recognizes and reports changes in condition; calls 911 first in an emergency; contacts the RN and family or representative; completes the report the same day.
Responds within 1 hour; directs the response; assesses within 48 hours of a significant change (or 7 calendar days if documented as unnecessary); updates the plan of care; keeps the on-call log.
Makes sure 24/7 on-call coverage is staffed; reviews events; ensures reports are filed.
Takes and relays calls, and keeps on-call numbers current for staff and clients.

documentation: Caregiver training and competency records on recognizing change in condition and emergency response
Incident or change-in-condition report
On-call log (time of call, caller, client, concern, action)
RN assessment note, with the reason documented if the 7-calendar-day timeframe is used
Updated plan of care
Advance directive information in the client record
Event review notes

policies.title: Discharge, Transfer and Discontinuation of Services
policies.applies_to: Administrator, RN Supervisor, scheduler, billing and records staff, and all clients served by the agency
policies.purpose: To make sure that services end, transfer or change only in a safe, orderly and authorized way, that the participant is consulted, that the transition is planned, and that the record is completed and kept as the regulations require.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not suspend, terminate, increase or reduce Medicaid personal assistance services without Department authorization and consultation with the participant. When services end or change, the agency sends a transition plan to the participant and to the case manager or supports planner. A client may stop services at any time. If the agency closes, changes ownership, location, name or tax ID, or is sold, it gives MDH 45 days' written notice that includes how participants will be informed and a transition plan for each of them. The record of a discharged client is completed within 30 days of discharge and kept as required by REC-01.

definitions.definition: The end of all agency services to a client.
Moving a client's services to another provider or level of care.
A written plan describing how the client's needs will continue to be met when services end or move, including the people responsible, dates and the client's choices.
The person who coordinates the participant's plan of service and authorized services under the Medicaid program.

procedures: The RN Supervisor or Administrator identifies the reason for any proposed discharge, transfer or reduction. Acceptable reasons include goals met, the client's request, the client moving or entering a facility, hospitalization with no planned return, death, loss of eligibility or authorization, unsafe conditions that cannot be corrected, or non-payment by a private-pay client.

For a Medicaid participant, the agency does not end, reduce or increase services on its own. The Administrator contacts the case manager or supports planner and requests Department authorization, and the RN or Administrator talks with the participant about the proposed change. Both steps are documented.

If the client asks to stop services, the RN or Administrator records the request, confirms that the client understands the effects, and tells the case manager or supports planner within [NUMBER] business days. Under IC-01, the RN documents a risk/benefit discussion if the client declines recommended care.

For a private-pay client, written notice of the discharge and its reason is given to the client or representative as far ahead as possible and no later than the notice period in the service agreement (CR-06).

If there is an immediate threat to a client's or caregiver's safety, the RN or Administrator takes protective action, such as calling 911 or reporting under ENV-08. The agency then contacts the supports planner and the Department the same day to request authorization for the change and document it.

The RN prepares a written transition plan listing the client's current needs and services, the client's preferences, any new provider or service, equipment or medications, and key dates. The RN reviews it with the client or representative.
The Administrator sends the transition plan to the case manager or supports planner and to the participant, and records the date and method of sending.

The RN or Administrator confirms that the client has contact information for the next provider or community resources. Maryland Access Point (1-844-MAP-LINK) and OLTSS (410-767-1739) are given when the client needs help finding services.
With the client's written consent, the RN sends a copy of current care information to the receiving provider. Records are released only as permitted by CR-03.
The Scheduler cancels or reassigns shifts on the discharge date and tells the aides. The Billing Coordinator stops billing as of the last date of service and reconciles ISAS time.
The RN completes a discharge summary that includes the reason, date, client condition, services provided, transition plan and any follow-up. The RN signs and dates it within 7 days.
The Records Coordinator completes the client record, including all notes, signatures and the discharge summary, within 30 days of discharge. The record is then filed and kept under REC-01.

If the agency plans to close, change ownership, location, name or tax ID, or to sell, the Administrator gives MDH 45 days' written notice. The notice states how participants will be informed and includes a transition plan for each of them. The Administrator also tells every participant and every supports planner, and starts any needed new license or enrollment process under ADM-11 and ADM-13.

If the agency closes, the Administrator arranges for client records to be returned to clients or representatives or retained as required by REC-01, and records where they are stored and who may be contacted for them.
The Administrator reviews discharges quarterly and reports numbers, reasons and any complaints to the Quality Assurance Committee (ADM-08).

responsibilities.duty: Requests authorization and notifies the Department; gives 45 days' notice to MDH of closure, sale or other listed changes; arranges record custody.
Consults with the participant; prepares the transition plan and discharge summary; coordinates with the case manager or supports planner.
Ends or reassigns schedules; informs aides.
Stops billing at the last date of service; reconciles ISAS time.
Completes and files the discharge record within 30 days.

documentation: Reason for discharge, transfer or change, and consultation with the participant
Request for and receipt of Department authorization (Medicaid participants)
Written transition plan and proof that it was sent to the case manager or supports planner and participant
Discharge summary
Notice of discharge to private-pay clients
45-day notice to MDH and participant notification (closure, sale or other change)
Completed discharge record within 30 days

policies.title: Coordination with Medicaid Programs, Nurse Monitors and Payers
policies.applies_to: Administrator, RN Supervisor, intake and scheduling staff, Billing Coordinator and caregivers
policies.purpose: To make sure services to Medicaid participants are coordinated with the supports planner, the nurse monitor, the Department and other payers. This policy also makes sure the agency serves only eligible participants, bills only authorized services, and supports the participant's person-centered plan consistent with 42 CFR 441.301(c).
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] delivers personal assistance only to participants who are Medicaid eligible, meet an institutional level of care and live at home. The participant's plan of service names the agency the participant has chosen. The agency verifies Medicaid eligibility at the start of each month of service. It bills only services that are preauthorized in the plan of service and delivered consistent with it. It cooperates with supports planners and nurse monitors, and with MDH and OLTSS inspections, reviews and audits. The participant or representative signs at least monthly to verify that services were delivered. The agency refers participants to Maryland Access Point (1-844-MAP-LINK) and to OLTSS (410-767-1739) for personal emergency response systems and community resources. The agency respects the participant's choices in the plan of service, consistent with 42 CFR 441.301(c).

definitions.definition: The Medicaid plan developed with the participant and supports planner or case manager that authorizes the services, hours and provider.
A nurse monitoring provider designated by the Department who conducts monitoring contacts and visits with the participant. The agency coordinates with the participant's nurse monitor.
The person who helps the participant develop and update the plan of service and coordinates authorized services.
The Maryland Department of Health Office of Long Term Services and Supports, which administers Community First Choice, CPAS and the Community Options waiver.
Maryland Access Point, a resource for information on community services and supports.

procedures: At referral, the Intake Coordinator confirms that the participant has a plan of service, that the plan names [AGENCY NAME] as the chosen agency, and that the participant lives at home. The Intake Coordinator records the supports planner's name and contact information.

Before the first service and again on or before the first day of each service month, the Billing Coordinator verifies the participant's Medicaid eligibility through the Department's eligibility verification system. The date, result and staff initials are recorded. If eligibility is not confirmed, the Billing Coordinator notifies the Administrator and the supports planner, and services continue only as the Department directs.

The Intake Coordinator compares the plan of service with the hours and tasks the agency has accepted, before scheduling. Any difference is raised with the supports planner and not resolved by the agency alone.

The RN Supervisor assesses the participant under ADM-09 and PC-02 and develops worker instructions consistent with the plan of service. The RN sends relevant information to the supports planner, with the participant's consent.

The Scheduler staffs only authorized hours and does not provide or bill services that are not in the plan of service. If the participant needs more or fewer hours, the RN or Administrator asks the supports planner to request Department authorization before any change (see PC-10).

The RN Supervisor tells the participant's nurse monitor how to reach the agency. The agency cooperates with nurse monitor contact, which per MDH is every 6 months, and the in-person visit, which is every 12 months. The RN provides requested records and arranges access to the participant and caregivers.

When the nurse monitor or supports planner reports a concern, the RN Supervisor responds within [NUMBER] business days. The RN records the concern, the action taken and the outcome in the client record and informs the participant.

Each month, the Scheduler or RN Supervisor obtains the signature of the participant or representative verifying that services were delivered. A representative may sign only if that person is not assigned as the worker. The signed verification is kept in the client record and any refusal to sign is documented and reported to the Administrator.

When a participant needs a personal emergency response system or other community resources, the RN refers the participant to Maryland Access Point (1-844-MAP-LINK) and gives OLTSS (410-767-1739) as a contact. The referral is recorded.

The agency respects the participant's choices and preferences, including those about who works with them, when and how. The RN includes those preferences in worker instructions and the person-centered plan, consistent with 42 CFR 441.301(c).

For participants with other payers, such as private pay, long-term care insurance or other coverage, the Intake Coordinator confirms with the participant and the payer which services each pays for and records it. The agency does not bill two payers for the same service.

When MDH, OLTSS or another authority announces or begins an inspection, review or audit, the Administrator is notified immediately, responds by the deadline given, and provides the requested records and access. The Administrator logs the request, what was produced and when.

The Administrator reviews audit and review findings within 7 days and develops a corrective action plan that is shared with the Quality Assurance Committee (ADM-08). Any overpayment identified is repaid promptly, because the agency may not have unpaid overpayments.

The Administrator reviews the agency's compliance with the provider conditions each quarter (ADM-13), including the conflict of interest check and any event that could affect provider participation, and records the results.

responsibilities.duty: Oversees coordination with OLTSS and MDH; handles audits and inspections; sees that overpayments are repaid and corrective actions completed.
Confirms plan of service, agency choice and residence; records supports planner contact.
Assesses and develops worker instructions; coordinates with the nurse monitor and supports planner; makes community referrals.
Verifies Medicaid eligibility monthly; bills only authorized services.
Schedules authorized hours; obtains the monthly participant or representative signature.

documentation: Plan of service and name of supports planner or case manager
Monthly Medicaid eligibility verification log
Nurse monitor contacts and agency responses
Monthly participant or representative verification of services (signed)
Referrals to MAP and OLTSS
Audit, inspection and review requests, records produced and corrective action plans
Repayment records for any overpayments

policies.title: Informed Consent to Changes in the Agency's Recommended Plan of Care
policies.applies_to: Registered Nurse (RN) Supervisor, Administrator, intake staff and all clients and client representatives
policies.purpose: To make sure that a client who chooses a plan of care different from the one the agency recommends makes that choice with full information, that the right person gives consent, and that the decision is documented and respected without retaliation.
policies.policy: This policy meets COMAR 10.07.05.08 B(1)(d)(i), Application p.6 (Informed Consent): a client, or a client representative with legal authority to make legal decisions, signs an informed consent form consenting to changes to the agency's recommended plan of care. [AGENCY NAME] does not reduce, omit or change a recommended service at the client's request until the RN has held and documented a risk and benefit discussion, and the client or authorized representative has signed and dated the informed consent form, and a copy is in the client record. The information given covers the purpose of the recommended care, alternatives, side effects and benefits, cost, and the right to withdraw consent. A client's refusal of treatment is honored, and the client is never penalized or retaliated against for refusing. The alternative route in the Application, B(1)(d)(ii), is addressed in IC-02.
