definitions.definition: The services, frequency, staffing and safety measures that the agency's RN recommends after assessing the client.

The client's or authorized representative's voluntary, written agreement to a change in the recommended plan of care, given after the RN explains the purpose, alternatives, side effects and benefits, cost and right to withdraw.

A person recognized by the agency as having authority to act for the client. This is a guardian of the person or property, a person named in an advance directive, a surrogate decision maker, an agent under a power of attorney, a representative payee, or a person the competent client has designated in writing.

procedures: After assessment (ADM-09), the RN explains the recommended plan of care to the client or representative in plain language, with an interpreter if needed (CR-05).
If the client or representative asks for a change (for example fewer hours, no RN visits, or no assistance with a task), the RN does not make the change until steps 3 through 9 are complete.

Before any consent discussion, the RN confirms who may consent. If the client is competent, the client consents. If a representative acts, the RN confirms and records the representative's name and authority, or files the authorizing document, such as a guardianship order, power of attorney, advance directive or the client's written designation.
The agency does not honor a representative's decision that goes beyond the authority given in the document. The RN reviews the document and asks the Administrator if the authority is unclear.

The RN holds a documented risk and benefit discussion with the client or representative. It covers the purpose of the recommended service, the alternatives, the side effects and benefits, the cost, and the right to withdraw consent at any time.
The RN offers other options that could meet the client's goals, and asks the client what concerns lie behind the request.

The RN completes the Informed Consent form, which names the recommended service, the change requested, the risks and benefits discussed, and the date. The client or authorized representative signs and dates it. The RN signs and dates it as the person who held the discussion.
The RN gives a copy of the signed form to the client or representative and places a copy in the client record the same day.

The RN revises the plan of care under PC-02 to reflect the change and tells the caregiver and, with the client's permission, the physician, case manager or supports planner. The Scheduler changes the schedule only after the signed form is on file. For Medicaid participants, any change in authorized hours also follows PC-10 and PC-11.

If the client or representative refuses to sign, the RN records the refusal, the discussion held and the reason. The RN continues to provide the services the client has agreed to, and informs the Administrator.
The agency does not threaten, pressure or retaliate against a client for refusing a recommended service. The client may accept or reject any referred caregiver without retaliation.

The RN reviews each informed consent at the next supervisory visit and at every annual reassessment, and when the client's condition changes. The client may withdraw consent at any time, and the RN then restores the recommended plan of care and documents it.
If the client's condition changes so that the consented change may now be unsafe, the RN promptly reassesses (PC-09) and holds a new risk and benefit discussion.
The Quality Assurance Committee audits a sample of records quarterly for a complete, signed and dated consent form, an identified decision-maker and a documented discussion (ADM-08).

responsibilities.duty: Conducts and documents the risk and benefit discussion; completes and obtains signatures on the form; updates the plan of care.
Decides whether to accept the recommended plan and signs the form if choosing a change; the representative acts only within the authority granted.
Resolves questions about a representative's authority; ensures no retaliation; reviews audit results.
Changes schedules only after the signed form is on file.

documentation: Signed and dated Informed Consent form with copy in the client record
RN note of the risk and benefit discussion (purpose, alternatives, side effects and benefits, cost, right to withdraw)
Representative's name and authority, or copy of the authorizing document
Updated plan of care
Record of refusal to sign, if any
Quarterly audit results

policies.title: Consent to Assistance by Non-Licensed Staff with Routine Treatments and Self-Administration of Medications
policies.applies_to: Registered Nurse (RN) Supervisor, non-licensed caregivers, scheduler, Administrator and clients or representatives
policies.purpose: To make sure no non-licensed caregiver helps a client with routine treatments or with self-administration of medications unless the client has first given informed, written consent, and the tasks are clearly limited and supervised.
policies.policy: This policy meets COMAR 10.07.05.08 B(1)(d)(ii), Application p.6 (Informed Consent): a client signs an informed consent form consenting to assistance by a non-licensed individual with treatments of a routine nature, or with the self-administration of medications. Before a non-licensed caregiver assists with a routine treatment or with a client's self-administration of medications, the client signs and dates a consent form that lists the specific tasks. The form is kept in the client record. The consent is reviewed at each annual reassessment, and the client may withdraw it at any time without penalty. Assistance with self-administration means helping a client who directs and takes the medication personally. It is not administration of medications. Administering drugs requires licensed or certified staff and physician orders, and is governed by PC-03. The RN supervises staff who assist with self-administration on site at least every 3 months, or more often as the RN decides.

definitions.definition: A treatment of a routine nature that the RN has determined, in the plan of care, may safely be assisted by a trained non-licensed caregiver.
Help such as reminding, opening containers, handing the client the medication, or steadying the client while the client directs and takes his or her own medication. The client makes the decisions.
A caregiver who is not a licensed nurse or other licensed health professional.
Giving a medication to a client; this must be done by licensed or certified staff acting on physician orders and is outside the scope of this consent.

procedures: During the RN's assessment (ADM-09), the RN identifies any routine treatments or medication self-administration for which the client wants caregiver help, and decides whether a non-licensed caregiver may safely assist.

The RN explains to the client or representative what the caregiver will and will not do. The RN covers the purpose, alternatives (for example, family help, a pharmacy packaging service or licensed nursing), benefits and side effects, cost and the right to withdraw, as required for informed consent (IC-01).

The RN lists each task by name on the Consent form, for example 'reminds client to take medications', 'hands the client the pill organizer' or 'applies a routine topical treatment as directed'. The form names the client's medications or treatments as they appear on the label or order.

The client signs and dates the form before any non-licensed caregiver gives assistance. If the client has a representative with legal authority (IC-04), the representative signs. The RN signs and dates the form after the discussion.
The RN gives the client or representative a copy and files the original in the client record the same day. The caregiver's assignment sheet lists only the tasks on the consent form.
The RN trains the caregiver in the specific tasks, checks competency and records it under PER-06 before the caregiver first assists the client.

The caregiver assists only with consented tasks. If the client asks for help with something not on the form, or the task would amount to giving medication, the caregiver does not do it and calls the RN. The Administrator ensures that any administration of medication follows PC-03.

The caregiver documents each time the client is assisted, including the date and time, what was done, and any refusal, missed dose, error, adverse reaction or concern. The caregiver reports medication errors and adverse reactions to the RN immediately.

The RN supervises staff who assist with self-administration on site at least every 3 months, or more often if the RN decides. The RN reviews the medication record and caregiver technique, talks with the client, and documents the visit under ADM-10.
The RN reviews the consent form at each annual reassessment and whenever the client's condition, medications or treatments change. The client or representative re-signs if the tasks change.

The client or representative may withdraw consent at any time, orally or in writing. The caregiver stops the assistance, the RN records the withdrawal, revises the plan of care and tells the Scheduler and any caregivers. The client is not penalized or retaliated against.

If the client or representative will not consent, the caregiver does not assist with the task. The RN records the refusal and discusses the safety risks with the client, following IC-01 if the client declines recommended care.

The Quality Assurance Committee audits a sample of records each quarter to confirm that a signed, dated consent form with listed tasks is on file for every client who receives this assistance, and that annual reviews were done (ADM-08).

responsibilities.duty: Decides which tasks non-licensed staff may assist with; explains and obtains consent; trains caregivers; supervises on site at least every 3 months; reviews consent annually.
Assists only with the tasks on the signed consent form; documents each assistance; reports errors, reactions and refusals to the RN at once.
Decides whether to consent; signs the form; may withdraw at any time.
Ensures no assistance starts without a signed form; reviews audits; ensures drug administration follows PC-03.

documentation: Signed and dated consent form listing the specific tasks, kept in the client record
RN note of the consent discussion
Caregiver training and competency record for the tasks
Caregiver documentation of assistance, refusals, errors and adverse reactions
RN on-site supervision notes (at least every 3 months)
Annual review of consent and any withdrawal of consent
Quarterly audit results

policies.title: Waiver of Skilled Services and Certified Caregiver
policies.applies_to: Supervising RN, Administrator, intake and scheduling staff, and all caregivers
policies.purpose: To set out when and how [AGENCY NAME] allows a client to decline skilled services or a certified caregiver, so the decision is informed, voluntary, documented and reviewed. The policy implements the waiver requirements in COMAR 10.07.05.10, 10.07.05.12 and 10.07.05.16.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] honors a client's informed decision to waive skilled services or a certified caregiver. A waiver is accepted only from a client who has decision-making capacity, or from a representative who has authority to make that decision (see IC-04). It is accepted only after the supervising RN has held a documented risk/benefit discussion with the client or representative. The waiver must be on a signed and dated form, and a copy must be in the client record. The agency will not accept a waiver that is incomplete, unsigned or undated, and will not use a waiver to cover a gap in staffing. Under COMAR 10.07.05.10, a non-certified caregiver may be assigned only in one of three situations: (1) the client needs no help with activities of daily living (ADLs); (2) the client needs ADL help, but in the supervising nurse's judgment there are no predictable adverse health consequences; or (3) the client or representative signs a waiver of skilled services. A certified caregiver is required for a client who needs one for ADLs or for medication administration, unless a valid waiver is in the record. A waiver does not allow non-licensed or non-certified staff to administer medications, which requires licensed or certified staff and physician orders (see PC-03). A waiver does not allow any caregiver to perform tasks outside the scope in ADM-02. Clients may accept or reject any referred caregiver without retaliation. The RN reviews every waiver at each reassessment. A client may withdraw a waiver at any time.

definitions.definition: A signed, dated written statement by which a client or authorized representative, after an RN risk/benefit discussion, declines skilled nursing services or a certified caregiver that the agency would otherwise recommend.
A caregiver who holds the certification Maryland requires for the task, with the certification verified by the agency before assignment (see PER-02 and PER-03).
A caregiver who is not certified and who may be assigned only in the situations described in the Policy section.
Basic self-care tasks such as bathing, dressing, toileting, transferring, mobility and eating.
A person recognized under IC-04 who has legal authority to make the decision on the client's behalf.

procedures: During the pre-acceptance assessment (ADM-06) and the initial RN assessment (ADM-09), the supervising RN determines whether the client needs ADL help, whether a certified caregiver is needed, and whether the client has skilled needs. The RN records the findings in the assessment.

If the client needs no ADL help, or needs ADL help with no predictable adverse health consequences, the RN documents that judgment in the record. A non-certified caregiver may then be assigned without a waiver.

If the client needs a certified caregiver or skilled services and declines them, or if the agency cannot meet the need, the RN offers the waiver option. The RN does not suggest or pressure a client to waive. The RN does not offer a waiver to cover for staffing shortages.

Before the discussion, the RN confirms who may decide. The RN confirms the client has capacity, or confirms the representative's authority under IC-04 and places the authorizing document or the representative's name in the record.

The RN holds the risk/benefit discussion with the client or representative, in the client's preferred language or with an interpreter as required by CR-05. The discussion covers: the purpose of the skilled service or certified caregiver; the likely benefits; the risks and possible side effects of going without; the alternatives; the cost; and the right to withdraw the waiver at any time.
The RN allows time for questions and invites the client to include family or another support person. The RN confirms the client or representative understands the decision.

The client or representative signs and dates the waiver form. The RN signs and dates it. The agency gives a copy to the client or representative and places a copy in the client record before a non-certified caregiver is assigned under the waiver.
The RN writes a note in the record that describes the discussion, the client's questions, the decision and the RN's assessment of understanding.

If the client or representative will not sign, the RN does not assign a non-certified caregiver unless the situations in the Policy section apply without a waiver. The RN then reviews with the Administrator whether the agency can safely serve the client under ADM-05, and if not, follows PC-10.
The RN records the waiver and its limits in the service plan (PC-02). The scheduler assigns a non-certified caregiver to a waiver client only after confirming that the signed waiver is in the record.
The RN explains to the client that the waiver does not allow non-licensed or non-certified staff to administer medications. Medication administration follows PC-03 and IC-02.
The agency honors the waiver. It does not reduce, delay or change services, and it does not retaliate against the client for waiving or for withdrawing a waiver.

At every reassessment (on request, at least annually, and after a significant change in condition), the RN reviews the waiver. The RN documents whether the client still wishes to waive, whether the client's condition or risks have changed, and whether a new risk/benefit discussion and a new signed form are needed. A new form is required if the scope of the waiver changes.

Caregivers report any change in the client's condition to the RN immediately (PC-09). The RN reassesses within 48 hours for a listed skilled need or significant change, or within 7 calendar days if the RN documents that the 48-hour assessment is unnecessary, and reconsiders the waiver.
During on-site supervisory visits (at least every 4 months, or more often as ADM-10 requires), the RN confirms the waiver is still in effect and being followed.

If a client or representative withdraws a waiver, orally or in writing, the RN documents it, assesses the client on the client's request, and arranges a certified caregiver or the skilled service as soon as practical. The scheduler updates the schedule and the RN updates the service plan.
The Administrator reviews waiver files during quality assurance checks (ADM-08) to confirm each waiver is signed, dated, reviewed and filed.

responsibilities.duty: Determine need for a certified caregiver or skilled services, conduct the risk/benefit discussion, obtain the signed waiver, review it at each reassessment, and document each step.
Ensure the waiver process is followed, resolve cases where the agency cannot safely serve a client, and audit waiver files.
Assign a non-certified caregiver to a waiver client only when a signed waiver is in the record, and update assignments when a waiver is withdrawn.
Work only within the service plan and ADM-02, never administer medications unless licensed or certified, and report changes in condition to the RN immediately.

documentation: Signed and dated waiver form (client or representative and RN), with a copy in the client record and a copy given to the client
RN note documenting the risk/benefit discussion, questions and understanding
RN documentation of the judgment that a non-certified caregiver is acceptable without a waiver, where applicable
Representative's name or authorizing document (IC-04)
Reassessment and supervisory visit notes showing waiver review
Notice of withdrawal of a waiver and the resulting service plan change

policies.title: Client Representatives and Advance Directives
policies.applies_to: Administrator, supervising RN, intake and scheduling staff, and all caregivers
policies.purpose: To ensure [AGENCY NAME] recognizes the right people to act for a client, never honors a representative who exceeds granted authority, and provides and obtains advance directive information as required by COMAR 10.07.05.13 and 10.07.05.16.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] recognizes as a client representative a guardian of the person or property, a person acting under an advance directive, a surrogate decision maker, an agent under a power of attorney, a representative payee, or a person a competent client has designated in writing. The agency honors a representative only within the authority granted. It does not honor a representative who exceeds that authority. The agency documents the representative's name in the record or keeps the authorizing document in the record. Where federal privacy rules apply, the agency treats a person with legal authority to make health care decisions for the client as the client's personal representative for purposes of 45 CFR 164.502(g), only to the extent of that authority (see CR-03). At admission the agency gives every client written information about advance directives and asks whether the client has one. If the client does, the agency obtains the information and a copy for the record. The agency does not make receipt of services depend on whether the client has an advance directive. The agency honors a client's refusal of treatment, and a waiver of skilled services under IC-03, whether made by the client or a properly authorized representative.

definitions.definition: A guardian of the person or property, a person acting under an advance directive, a surrogate decision maker, an agent under a power of attorney, a representative payee, or a person designated in writing by a competent client.
A written or oral instruction recognized under Maryland law about future health care decisions or about who may make them if the client cannot.
A person or organization appointed to manage a client's benefit payments. This role may not cover health care decisions.
The decisions the authorizing document or legal order allows the representative to make.

procedures: At intake (ADM-05), the intake coordinator asks the client whether he or she has a guardian, advance directive, surrogate, power of attorney, representative payee, or a person the client wants designated to act or receive information.

If the client has capacity and wishes to designate someone, the intake coordinator has the client sign a written designation naming the person and stating what the person may decide or receive. The designation is dated and kept in the record.

For any other representative, the intake coordinator requests a copy of the authorizing document (court order, power of attorney, advance directive, payee appointment) and places it in the record. If no document exists, the coordinator records the representative's name, relationship and the basis for recognition. The Administrator approves the record entry.

The RN reads the document and notes the scope of authority on the client face sheet, for example 'financial only' or 'health care decisions'. The scheduler and caregivers use the face sheet to know whom to contact.

Staff accept decisions, consents and waivers from the representative only for matters within the documented scope. If a representative asks for something outside that authority, the staff member declines, tells the RN, and the RN informs the Administrator.

If the Administrator believes a representative is exceeding authority or acting against the client's wishes or interests, the Administrator consults [LEGAL COUNSEL/ORGANIZATION CONTACT] and, if there is a concern about abuse or exploitation, follows ENV-08.
At admission, the RN or intake coordinator gives the client or representative written advance directive information and explains that the agency does not condition services on having a directive.

The RN asks whether the client has an advance directive, such as a living will, health care agent appointment or Maryland MOLST form, and documents the answer. If the client has one, the RN obtains a copy, places it in the record, and notes where the original is kept.

If the client has no directive and wants information or to complete one, the RN provides written information and suggests the client speak with a physician, attorney or other qualified person. The agency staff do not give legal advice and do not witness or sign directives on the client's behalf.

Caregivers are told, in orientation (PER-06), that they do not interpret directives or decide what a directive requires. In an emergency they follow the emergency steps in PC-09 and ENV-05, including calling 911, and tell emergency responders about any directive or MOLST form kept in the home.
When a client who was competent loses capacity, the RN notifies the Administrator, identifies any representative named in a directive or power of attorney, and updates the record.
At each reassessment, the RN asks whether any representative, directive or designation has changed and updates the record. New or revoked documents are filed with the date received.
Protected health information is shared with a representative only as allowed by CR-03 and 45 CFR 164.502(g). Staff verify the person's identity and authority before disclosing anything.
The Administrator checks a sample of records each quarter under ADM-08 to confirm that each file contains the representative's name or authorizing document and advance directive information.

responsibilities.duty: Ask about representatives and directives at intake, collect and file documents or designations, and give advance directive information.
Read documents, record scope of authority, obtain the client's advance directive information, and update at each reassessment.
Decide disputed cases, refuse requests that exceed authority, and audit records.
Contact the right person, never accept decisions outside a representative's authority, and follow emergency procedures without interpreting directives.

documentation: Representative's name and relationship, or the authorizing document, in the client record
Client's written designation of a representative, signed and dated
Face sheet note of the scope of the representative's authority
Receipt of advance directive information and the client's answer, plus a copy of any directive or MOLST
Record of any refused request that exceeded a representative's authority
Updates at each reassessment

policies.title: Preparation and Storage of Enteral Formulas, IV Therapies, Supplies and Equipment
policies.applies_to: Administrator, supervising RN, scheduler and all caregivers
policies.purpose: To state how [AGENCY NAME] handles the preparation and storage of enteral formulas, intravenous (IV) therapies, other supplies and equipment, and similar items. It protects clients by keeping these tasks away from unqualified staff. This policy meets COMAR 10.07.05.08B(1)(e)(i), Application p.6 (Environment and Safety), item B(1)(e)(i): preparation and storage of enteral formulas, intravenous therapies, other supplies, equipment, and similar items.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not prepare or store enteral formulas or IV therapies, and caregivers must not handle them. This includes mixing, measuring, warming, hanging, connecting, flushing, starting, stopping, adjusting or storing formulas, solutions, tubing, pumps or IV access devices. Caregivers may keep routine client supplies, such as incontinence products, gloves, wipes and basic personal care supplies, clean, dry and separate from food. Caregivers report supply problems to the RN. If the agency decides to add enteral, IV or similar services, the agency will first write a preparation and storage procedure that covers formula and medication handling, labeling, temperature, expiration, cleaning of equipment and who is qualified to perform each task. The agency will update this manual and notify OHCQ as required by ADM-11 before beginning those services.

definitions.definition: Liquid nutrition given through a feeding tube into the stomach or intestine.
Fluids, nutrition or medication given directly into a vein, including by pump or port.
Non-sterile, non-prescription items used in everyday personal care, such as incontinence products, gloves, wipes, lotions and basic cleaning supplies.
Devices used in a client's care, whether owned by the client or the agency. See ENV-04.

procedures: During the pre-acceptance assessment (ADM-06), the RN asks whether the client uses enteral feeding, IV therapy or similar treatment. The RN documents the answer.

If the client needs a service the agency does not provide, such as formula preparation or IV care, the RN explains to the client or representative that agency caregivers will not perform it and who will, such as the client's nurse, family or another provider. The RN documents the discussion (ADM-03 and ADM-04).

If another provider or family member manages the therapy, the service plan (PC-02) states that agency caregivers do not prepare, store, hang, adjust, flush or disconnect formulas or IV therapies. The service plan also states what caregivers may do, such as routine personal care.

In orientation (PER-06), the RN trains caregivers that they do not touch, move or adjust formulas, IV bags, tubing, pumps or feeding or IV access devices. Caregivers must not troubleshoot alarms or reposition tubes.
If a client asks a caregiver to handle or prepare a formula or IV therapy, the caregiver declines politely, does not do the task, and tells the RN the same day.

If a pump alarms, a tube comes out, a line leaks or the client has signs of distress, the caregiver does not intervene. The caregiver calls the RN or on-call number (ADM-10). If the situation is an emergency, the caregiver calls 911 and follows PC-09.
Caregivers store routine client supplies in a clean, dry place, away from food and food preparation surfaces and away from cleaning chemicals and medications where practical.

Caregivers check routine supplies for damage, moisture or an expired or opened package at each visit. Caregivers do not use damaged supplies. They report shortages, damaged supplies and storage problems to the RN, who contacts the client or representative or the supplier.
Caregivers do not buy supplies except as the service plan allows and CR-04 permits.

If the agency considers adding enteral, IV or similar services, the Administrator and RN must write the preparation and storage procedure, training, competency checks and staffing requirements, and obtain governing authority approval (ADM-01) before the service is offered. The agency updates this policy at that time.
The RN reviews compliance during supervisory visits (ADM-10) and records any concerns.
The Administrator reviews this policy at the annual policy review (ADM-01).

responsibilities.duty: Screen for enteral and IV needs, write the service plan limits, train caregivers, and respond to supply or alarm calls.
Ensure no enteral or IV services are provided and approve any future addition of such services.
Never handle formulas, IV therapies or related devices; store routine supplies properly; report problems to the RN.
Do not schedule caregivers for any task involving enteral or IV preparation or handling.

documentation: Pre-acceptance assessment entry on enteral and IV needs
Service plan statement of the limits on caregiver tasks
Record of the RN's explanation to the client or representative about services the agency does not provide
Caregiver reports about requests, alarms or supply problems
Orientation and training records (PER-06)

policies.title: Infection Prevention and Control
policies.applies_to: All caregivers, supervising RN, scheduler and Administrator
policies.purpose: To protect clients and staff from infection through standard precautions and exposure controls. This policy meets COMAR 10.07.05.08B(1)(e)(ii), Application p.6, item B(1)(e)(ii): infection control procedures. It also meets the standard precautions training content in COMAR 10.07.05.11 and the OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard, 29 CFR 1910.1030.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] requires all staff to use standard precautions with every client, every time. All caregivers are trained in standard precautions at orientation and annually. The agency follows a written Exposure Control Plan under 29 CFR 1910.1030. The plan covers: identification of tasks with possible exposure; hand hygiene; gloves and other protective equipment; cleaning and laundry; sharps rules; hepatitis B vaccine offer; exposure incident response; training; and recordkeeping. The agency supplies gloves and other protective equipment at no cost to staff. Staff with symptoms of a possible infectious illness stay out of client homes. Any exposure incident is reported immediately and handled under the procedures below.

definitions.definition: Infection-prevention practices applied to all clients, including hand hygiene, gloves and other protective equipment when contact with blood or body fluids is likely, safe handling of soiled items, and cleaning of surfaces.
A specific eye, mouth, other mucous membrane, non-intact skin or parenteral contact with blood or other potentially infectious material that results from the performance of an employee's duties.
The agency's written OSHA plan describing how it identifies, reduces and responds to occupational exposure to blood and other potentially infectious materials.
Needles, lancets, razors with blood, or other objects that can puncture or cut skin.

procedures: The Administrator and RN maintain a written Exposure Control Plan that meets 29 CFR 1910.1030. They review and update it at least annually and when tasks or procedures change. The plan is available to any employee on request.

At orientation and annually (PER-06), the RN trains every caregiver on standard precautions, hand hygiene, glove use, safe cleaning and laundry, sharps rules, exposure reporting and the Exposure Control Plan. The RN documents attendance and competency in the personnel file.

Caregivers perform hand hygiene (soap and water, or alcohol-based rub when hands are not visibly soiled) when arriving, before and after client contact, before and after glove use, after toileting or handling soiled items, before preparing food, and when leaving the home. Soap and water is required when hands are visibly soiled.

Caregivers wear disposable gloves whenever contact with blood, body fluids, mucous membranes, non-intact skin or soiled items is likely. They change gloves between tasks and between clients, and never reuse them. Caregivers use gowns, masks or eye protection when splashes are likely, as the RN instructs.

Caregivers clean and disinfect frequently touched surfaces and soiled areas with the cleaning product the RN approves, following the label's contact time. They clean from clean to dirty areas, and do not mix chemicals.

Caregivers handle laundry as follows: wear gloves for soiled linen and clothing, avoid shaking it, bag it at the point of use, and wash it with hot water and detergent as the product and fabric allow. Caregivers keep soiled and clean linen separate.
Caregivers do not recap, bend, break or handle sharps (see ENV-03). If a sharp is found, they leave it, keep others away and call the RN.
Caregivers keep personal items such as food and drinks separate from soiled items. They do not eat or drink while handling soiled items.

Staff who have fever, vomiting, diarrhea, a new cough or sore throat, a rash that might be contagious, draining skin lesions or any other symptom of a possible infectious illness must call the scheduler and stay out of client homes until the RN or Administrator clears them to work. The scheduler arranges coverage. Staff may not be penalized for reporting symptoms (see PER-08).
Caregivers tell the RN promptly if a client has symptoms of infection or a diagnosed communicable disease. The RN gives instructions on precautions and reports as required (PC-09).

After any exposure incident, the employee immediately washes the area with soap and water (or flushes eyes or mucous membranes with water) and calls the RN or on-call number at once. The RN arranges prompt confidential medical evaluation and follow-up as the OSHA standard requires, and documents the circumstances, the source, and the evaluation. The employee also completes an incident report (ENV-09).
The agency offers hepatitis B vaccination to caregivers with occupational exposure within the time the OSHA standard requires, at no cost. Employees who decline sign a declination.
The agency keeps training records and confidential exposure and medical records as 29 CFR 1910.1030 requires. Training records go in the personnel file (PER-07).
The Administrator reviews exposure incidents and compliance during quality assurance (ADM-08) and reviews this policy at the annual policy review (ADM-01).
Tuberculosis screening of staff follows PER-05.

responsibilities.duty: Maintain and annually review the Exposure Control Plan, provide protective equipment and vaccine, and ensure recordkeeping.
Train caregivers, respond to exposure incidents, arrange follow-up evaluation, and advise on precautions for clients with infections.
Use standard precautions every time, follow sharps and laundry rules, stay home when symptomatic, and report exposures immediately.
Arrange coverage when staff report symptoms and never pressure a symptomatic employee to work.

documentation: Written Exposure Control Plan with annual review dates
Orientation and annual training records for standard precautions and exposure control
Hepatitis B vaccine offers, acceptances and declinations
Exposure incident reports and follow-up evaluation records, kept confidentially
Staff illness call logs and return-to-work clearances
QA review of infection control and exposure incidents

policies.title: Disposal of Biomedical Waste
policies.applies_to: All caregivers, supervising RN and Administrator
policies.purpose: To explain how [AGENCY NAME] keeps staff and clients safe from biomedical waste and sharps. This policy meets COMAR 10.07.05.08B(1)(e)(iii), Application p.6, item B(1)(e)(iii): disposal of biomedical waste. It also supports the standard precautions training in COMAR 10.07.05.11 and 29 CFR 1910.1030.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not generate biomedical waste, and its aides do not handle sharps. Caregivers may handle ordinary contaminated items from personal care, such as soiled incontinence products, wipes and used gloves. They double-bag these items and put them in household trash only when the RN confirms that is permitted for that client and situation. Caregivers never recap, bend, break, pick up or move sharps. If they find or are made aware of a sharp, they do not touch it, they call the RN, and the RN decides what to do. Any needlestick or other sharps injury is reported at once as an exposure incident under ENV-02 and ENV-09.

definitions.definition: Waste that may carry infection, such as blood-soaked items, sharps and materials from medical procedures. This does not include ordinary soiled personal care items that the RN has confirmed may go in household trash.
Needles, syringes, lancets and other objects that can puncture or cut skin and may carry blood or other infectious material.
A rigid, puncture-resistant, closable container for used sharps, owned and managed by the client, family or the client's licensed provider.
Contact with blood or other potentially infectious material through eyes, mouth, mucous membranes, non-intact skin or a puncture while on duty (see ENV-02).

procedures: During the pre-acceptance assessment (ADM-06), the RN asks whether the client uses needles, injectables, lancets or other sharps, or produces other medical waste. The RN documents the answer and who handles it, such as the client, family or a nurse.

If the client has sharps or medical waste, the RN tells the client or representative that agency caregivers will not handle it. The RN also explains the plan for its disposal, using the client's other providers or the client's pharmacist or physician where needed, and records the plan in the service plan (PC-02).
In orientation (PER-06), the RN trains caregivers to recognize sharps and medical waste, never to touch them, and what to do if they find them.

For ordinary soiled items such as incontinence products, wipes and used gloves, the caregiver wears gloves, places the item in a leak-resistant bag, ties it, places that bag in a second bag, and ties it.

The caregiver places the double-bagged item in household trash only if the RN has confirmed it is permitted. If the RN has not confirmed it, the caregiver keeps the item bagged and calls the RN for instruction.

If an item is saturated or dripping with blood or body fluid, the caregiver does not put it in household trash. The caregiver contains it in a bag, keeps it away from others and calls the RN, who gives instructions based on the situation.

Caregivers never recap, bend, break, remove or pick up used needles, lancets or other sharps. They do not put their hands into a sharps container or trash that may contain sharps, and they do not compress trash by hand.

If a caregiver finds a loose sharp, or the sharps container is full, overflowing or damaged, the caregiver does not touch it, keeps the client and others away from it, and calls the RN right away. The RN directs the client or representative, or the client's nurse, to dispose of it safely, and documents the call.

If a caregiver is stuck by a needle or cut by a sharp, the caregiver immediately washes the area with soap and water, calls the RN or on-call number, and follows the exposure incident steps in ENV-02. The RN arranges follow-up care, and the caregiver files an incident report (ENV-09).
The RN reviews any report involving sharps or biomedical waste and updates the client's service plan to prevent a recurrence.
The Administrator reviews incidents involving sharps during QA (ADM-08) and reviews this policy at the annual policy review (ADM-01).

responsibilities.duty: Screen for sharps and medical waste, confirm what may go into household trash, respond to caregiver calls, and arrange exposure follow-up.
Double-bag ordinary soiled items, never handle sharps, call the RN, and report any needlestick immediately.
Ensure staff training, supply of gloves and bags, incident review and annual policy review.

documentation: Pre-acceptance assessment entry on sharps and medical waste
Service plan note on who manages sharps or medical waste
RN notes on caregiver calls about waste or sharps
Exposure incident reports and follow-up records (ENV-02, ENV-09)
Orientation and training records (PER-06)

policies.title: Maintenance of Equipment
policies.applies_to: All caregivers, supervising RN, scheduler and Administrator
policies.purpose: To keep equipment used in client care safe, clean and working. This policy meets COMAR 10.07.05.08B(1)(e)(iv), Application p.6, item B(1)(e)(iv): maintenance of equipment, and the procedures that go with it (the application words the item 'Maintenance of equipment; and procedures'; COMAR reads 'Maintenance of equipment'). The procedures are in the Procedures section below.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] inspects and cleans agency-owned equipment, such as gait belts and lifts if used, between clients. Caregivers do not repair client-owned equipment. They report malfunctions to the RN. Defective equipment is removed from use and the removal is documented. Questions about replacement of a personal emergency response system (PERS) are directed to Maryland Access Point (MAP) or the Office of Long Term Services and Supports (OLTSS).

definitions.definition: Equipment the agency buys or supplies for caregiver use with clients, such as gait belts and, if the agency uses them, lifts.
Equipment the client, family or another provider owns or supplies, such as wheelchairs, walkers, hospital beds, commodes and PERS devices.
Personal emergency response system, a device a client uses to call for help.
Maryland Access Point, the state's resource and referral network for long-term services and supports.
The Maryland Department of Health's Office of Long Term Services and Supports, telephone 410-767-1739.

procedures: The RN keeps a list of agency-owned equipment and the cleaning and inspection instructions for each item. Caregivers receive training on use, inspection and cleaning of each item at orientation (PER-06).
Before each use, the caregiver inspects agency-owned equipment for cracks, fraying, damaged buckles or fasteners, loose parts or other damage. A gait belt must be intact and the buckle must hold.

After each use and before use with another client, the caregiver cleans and disinfects agency-owned equipment with the product and contact time the RN has approved (ENV-02). Cloth items that cannot be disinfected are laundered or assigned to one client only.
Caregivers store agency-owned equipment clean and dry, away from soiled items.

If agency-owned equipment is defective or damaged, the caregiver stops using it, tags it 'Do Not Use', and tells the RN the same day. The RN removes it from service, arranges repair or replacement, and records the removal on the equipment log.
Caregivers inspect client-owned equipment visually during use. They do not repair, adjust, modify or assemble it, and they do not use equipment that looks unsafe.

If client-owned equipment is broken, unstable, or not working, the caregiver tells the client or representative that it should not be used, stops any task that depends on it, and reports it to the RN right away. The caregiver uses safer alternatives only as the RN directs.

The RN contacts the client or representative, the equipment supplier or the client's provider to arrange repair or replacement, and documents the call and the outcome. If the problem creates a safety risk, the RN updates the service plan (PC-02) and, as needed, follows PC-09.

If a PERS device does not work or needs replacement, the RN or intake coordinator tells the client or representative to contact the PERS provider and refers questions about replacement or funding to MAP or OLTSS (410-767-1739). The RN documents the referral and checks at the next contact that the client has a working PERS.

If someone is injured or nearly injured because of equipment, the caregiver reports it to the RN at once and completes an incident report (ENV-09). In an emergency the caregiver follows PC-09 and calls 911.
The RN reviews equipment logs and equipment safety at supervisory visits (ADM-10) and during quality assurance (ADM-08). The Administrator reviews this policy at the annual policy review (ADM-01).

responsibilities.duty: Maintain the equipment list and log, train staff, remove defective agency equipment, and follow up on client-owned equipment problems.
Inspect and clean agency equipment, never repair client-owned equipment, stop using unsafe equipment and report defects to the RN the same day.
Fund repair or replacement of agency-owned equipment, review incidents and ensure annual policy review.
Notify the RN when a caregiver reports equipment problems and adjust schedules as the RN directs.

documentation: Agency-owned equipment list and cleaning and inspection log
Records of defective equipment removed from use, repairs and replacements
Caregiver reports and RN notes about client-owned equipment problems
Referrals to MAP or OLTSS concerning PERS
Incident reports for equipment-related injuries (ENV-09)
Orientation and training records (PER-06)

policies.title: Emergency Procedures, Client Emergency and Disaster Plans
policies.applies_to: All clients, caregivers, supervising nurses, on-call staff and office staff
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] can protect clients and keep services going during medical emergencies, power outages, evacuations, severe weather, office closures and staff shortages, and that every client and caregiver knows what to do and whom to call.
policies.policy: This policy meets COMAR 10.07.05.08B(1)(e)(v) — Environment and Safety, Emergency procedures (OHCQ application p.6, item B(1)(e)(v)). [AGENCY NAME] maintains written emergency procedures for the agency and an individual emergency/disaster plan for every client. The agency covers the following: (1) a client emergency/disaster plan completed at intake, covering evacuation, medical emergency and power outage; (2) agency procedures for office closure, staff shortage and severe weather; (3) a 24-hour, 7-day on-call line with a response within 1 hour, a call log, and written on-call procedures given to each client (COMAR 10.07.05.12); (4) a priority list of the clients at highest risk; and (5) backup caregivers identified for each client. Caregivers call 911 first for any life-threatening emergency and never delay emergency care to contact the agency. Caregivers do not give care outside their training in an emergency; they summon help, give first aid or CPR within their training, and stay with the client until help arrives.

definitions.definition: A written plan, kept in the client record and a copy left in the home, listing evacuation routes and meeting place, who to call, medical conditions, medications and equipment, power-dependent equipment, backup caregivers, and the client's preferences in an emergency.

A client who would be in immediate danger if a visit were missed or delayed or if power or transport failed, for example someone who is bed-bound, lives alone, uses oxygen or other power-dependent equipment, has cognitive impairment, or has no family or other support nearby.
A qualified, screened and oriented caregiver identified in advance to cover a client's visits if the assigned caregiver cannot work.
The agency telephone number answered by a qualified staff member 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.

procedures: At intake, before or at the start of services, the intake coordinator or RN explains the emergency plan process to the client or representative and gives the client the agency's written on-call procedures and 24/7 phone number, [PHONE].

At the RN assessment, the RN completes the client emergency/disaster plan with the client or representative. It addresses (a) evacuation, including mobility limits, stairs, and who can help; (b) medical emergency, including diagnoses, allergies, medications, physician and emergency contacts, and any advance directive on file (see IC-04); and (c) power outage, including oxygen, suction, lift, bed, or other powered equipment and alternatives.
The RN records the client's closest relative or other emergency contact, the neighbor or friend who could assist, the local utility, and the nearest hospital preferred by the client.

The RN asks whether the client has a personal emergency response system (PERS). If not and the client may benefit, the RN or care coordinator refers the client or case manager to Maryland Access Point (1-844-MAP-LINK) or the Office of Long Term Services and Supports (410-767-1739) for PERS and community resources.

The RN assigns each client a risk level (high, moderate or standard) based on the assessment and records it in the record. The care coordinator keeps a priority list of high-risk clients, with phone numbers, address, equipment and emergency contacts, available to the on-call staff member at all times.

The scheduler identifies at least one backup caregiver for each client, records the name in the schedule system, and confirms that the backup meets the qualifications for that client's plan of care (see PER-02 and PC-07).

The RN signs and dates the emergency plan, gives a copy to the client or representative, and places the copy in the client record. The caregiver reviews the plan at the first visit and the supervisor confirms this in writing.

The RN reviews and updates the plan whenever there is a significant change in condition, a change in equipment or home, a change in caregiver or emergency contacts, and at least at the annual reassessment (COMAR 10.07.05.12).

On-call coverage: [AGENCY NAME] keeps a qualified on-call staff member available by phone 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. The on-call staff member responds to every call within 1 hour. Each call is entered in the on-call log with date, time, caller, concern, action taken, follow-up and the name of the person responding. The administrator reviews the log at least monthly.

Medical emergency in the home: the caregiver calls 911 for any life-threatening condition, gives first aid or CPR within training, calls the on-call line as soon as the client is safe, stays with the client until help arrives, and gives emergency personnel the client's medication list and emergency plan. The on-call RN notifies the representative and physician and directs follow-up under PC-09 and ENV-09.

Evacuation or loss of power: the caregiver follows the client's plan, moves the client to safety, uses backup equipment or an alternate arrangement identified in the plan, and calls the on-call line. The on-call staff member arranges additional help, alternate shelter or transport through the client's contacts or emergency services.

Severe weather and declared emergencies: when a storm, flood, extreme heat or cold, or an official emergency is forecast or declared, the administrator or designee activates this plan. The care coordinator contacts all high-risk clients, starting with the priority list, confirms staffing and visits, and records each contact. Caregivers do not travel when authorities have closed roads or ordered no travel; the agency then contacts the affected clients by phone, arranges alternate coverage where it is safe, and documents the missed visit and the reason.

Staff shortage: if the number of available caregivers falls below that needed to cover scheduled visits, the scheduler follows the priority list, assigns backup caregivers first to high-risk clients, notifies the RN and administrator, and contacts affected clients and case managers about any delayed or missed visit (PC-07). Visits are never covered by unqualified or unscreened staff.

Office closure: if the office is closed or unusable, the administrator moves operations to [ALTERNATE LOCATION OR REMOTE ACCESS], keeps the on-call line active by forwarding to a staff phone, and gives caregivers and clients the temporary contact information. Client records remain protected under CR-03 and REC-01.

After any activation of this plan, the administrator or designee holds a review within 14 days, documents what happened, what worked and what must change, and updates this policy or the client's plan. The review is reported to the Quality Assurance committee under ADM-08.
New caregivers are trained on this policy at orientation (PER-06). The agency reviews it annually with all staff, and tests the on-call process at least once per year, recording the date and results.

responsibilities.duty: Maintains and reviews this policy, activates it for office closures, severe weather and staff shortages, reviews the on-call log monthly, and keeps contact information current.
Completes and updates each client's emergency plan, assigns risk level, responds to on-call medical concerns and reviews incidents.
Maintains the priority list and backup caregivers, contacts high-risk clients during emergencies and documents missed visits.
Answers the line 24/7, responds within 1 hour, logs every call, and escalates to the RN or administrator.
Knows each client's plan, calls 911 in emergencies, reports to the on-call line, and documents events.
Helps develop the plan, keeps emergency contacts current and tells the agency about changes in the home or equipment.

documentation: Signed and dated client emergency/disaster plan in the record, with annual review
Risk level and priority list
Backup caregiver assignments
On-call log and written on-call procedures given to client (receipt in the record)
Records of contacts made during emergencies and any missed visits
Post-event reviews
Training and annual review records

policies.title: Caregiver Safety in the Home and Workplace Violence
policies.applies_to: All caregivers, supervising nurses, office staff and anyone who enters a client's home on behalf of the agency
policies.purpose: To protect the health and safety of caregivers and other staff in client homes and in the workplace, to prevent injury and violence, and to give staff a clear way to leave an unsafe situation without penalty.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides a workplace free of recognized hazards likely to cause death or serious physical harm, consistent with the OSH Act General Duty Clause. Home safety is reviewed at assessment. Caregivers may leave any home that is unsafe and must call the supervisor. Violence, threats and unsafe conditions are reported as incidents. Training covers body mechanics and safe transfers. These requirements are part of the agency's environment and safety policies under COMAR 10.07.05.08, and staff training content follows COMAR 10.07.05.11. No staff member is disciplined or retaliated against for leaving an unsafe home or for reporting a hazard in good faith.

definitions.definition: A condition in or around the home that presents a reasonable risk of physical harm, such as violence or threats, weapons displayed in a threatening way, impaired persons who are aggressive, active fire or gas leak, severe infestation, structural hazards, aggressive animals, or the presence of an unlawful activity.

Any physical assault, threat, harassment, intimidation or other disruptive behavior directed at staff by a client, family member, visitor, co-worker or other person, whether in a client's home or at the office.
A documented checklist completed by the RN at assessment that identifies hazards to the client and to staff.

procedures: At the RN assessment, the RN completes a home safety review covering entrances and lighting, stairs and walkways, clutter and trip hazards, smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, electrical and heating hazards, pests, pets, firearms and other weapons, smoking and oxygen, bathroom hazards, safe storage of chemicals, and any known history of violence by anyone in the home.

The RN records identified hazards in the record, tells the client or representative, asks for correction where possible, and writes safety measures into the service plan (see PC-02). Where hazards cannot be corrected, the RN consults the administrator on whether services can be provided safely.
Before a first visit, the scheduler gives the caregiver the address, access information, the safety information from the assessment, and the supervisor's contact number.

Caregivers use safe body mechanics, use assistive devices and equipment named in the service plan, and use two-person assistance when the plan requires it. A caregiver does not attempt a transfer or lift that exceeds their training or the plan and instead calls the supervisor.
Caregivers use standard precautions and personal protective equipment as required by ENV-02, and report needlesticks, exposures and injuries immediately.

If a caregiver feels threatened or finds an unsafe situation at any time, the caregiver may leave the home immediately. If anyone is in immediate danger, the caregiver calls 911. If the client cannot safely be left alone, the caregiver tells the 911 operator and the supervisor before leaving, if it is safe to do so.

As soon as the caregiver reaches a safe location, the caregiver calls the supervisor or on-call line, [PHONE], and reports what occurred. The supervisor documents the call and decides, with the RN and administrator, whether to resume, modify, suspend, or end services in line with PC-10 and Medicaid authorization rules where they apply.

The agency does not require a caregiver to return to a home where a safety concern remains unresolved. The caregiver is offered other assignments, and the client's visits are covered through backup arrangements (PC-07).

Every threat, assault, harassment, injury or hazard is reported to the supervisor the same day and documented as an incident under ENV-09. The supervisor notifies the administrator immediately for any physical violence, weapon or injury.

The administrator reviews each incident of violence, decides on follow-up (for example, a safety plan, two-person visits, a change in caregiver, law enforcement referral, or discharge) and informs the client or representative as appropriate.
Staff injured at work receive first aid or medical care, and the agency completes workers' compensation and any required injury reports. Staff are offered a debrief after violence or a threat.

Staff who work alone are given the on-call number, are told to share their schedule with the office, and may carry a charged phone. Caregivers do not enter a home where the client is not present unless the plan allows it.

Workplace violence among staff and at the office is handled the same way. Staff report to the administrator, or to the owner if the administrator is involved, who investigates, protects the reporting person from retaliation and documents the outcome.

Orientation and annual training include body mechanics, safe transfers and positioning, recognizing and de-escalating aggressive behavior, leaving an unsafe home, standard precautions, and reporting (PER-06 and COMAR 10.07.05.11 content). Training is documented with date, trainer and content.
The administrator reviews safety incidents and injuries at least quarterly and brings trends and corrective actions to the Quality Assurance review (ADM-08).

responsibilities.duty: Maintains this policy, investigates violence and serious injury, prevents retaliation and ensures training.
Completes the home safety review, writes safety measures in the service plan and trains caregivers on safe techniques.
Answers safety calls, directs the caregiver, documents events and arranges coverage.
Follows safe practices, leaves an unsafe home and calls the supervisor, and reports hazards, threats and injuries.
Maintains a reasonably safe home, secures pets and weapons during visits and does not threaten or harass staff.

documentation: Home safety review in the client record
Safety measures in the service plan
Incident reports for violence, threats, injuries and unsafe homes
On-call log entries
Training records for body mechanics, safe transfers and violence prevention
Records of administrator follow-up

policies.title: Transporting Clients
policies.applies_to: Caregivers, schedulers, supervising nurses and the administrator
policies.purpose: To state when, if ever, [AGENCY NAME] staff may transport clients, to protect clients and the agency from unpaid or unauthorized transport, and to make sure clients know what is and is not covered.
policies.policy: Escort and travel expenses are not covered by Medicaid personal assistance (COMAR 10.09.84.23). Caregivers do not transport clients in their own vehicles during Medicaid-covered time. [AGENCY NAME] provides transportation only as a private-pay service that is written into the service agreement, using a driver with a valid license and with insurance in place, including non-owned auto coverage for the agency. The cost of any private-pay transport and the fact that it is not covered by a third-party payer are disclosed to the client in writing before services start, in line with the client's right to a cost estimate and a statement of costs not covered by third parties (COMAR 10.07.05.16).

definitions.definition: Driving a client in any vehicle, including a caregiver's own car, an agency vehicle, or a client's vehicle.
Accompanying a client to an appointment, errand or outing.
Liability insurance held by the agency that covers accidents when staff use their own vehicles for agency business.

procedures: The intake coordinator tells every client or representative at intake that Medicaid personal assistance does not cover escort or travel expenses, and that caregivers do not drive clients during Medicaid-authorized time.

A caregiver who is asked to drive a Medicaid client, or to run an errand with the client in a vehicle, declines politely, explains the policy, and tells the supervisor. The caregiver does not accept money for this.

The scheduler does not bill, and the caregiver does not record, travel or driving time as Medicaid personal assistance time. Time spent at an appointment is not billed as Medicaid unless the activity is an authorized service in the plan of service and consistent with COMAR 10.09.84 limitations.
Where a client needs transport, the care coordinator refers the client or case manager to community or Medicaid transportation options and records the referral.

The agency may offer private-pay transport only when (a) the administrator has approved it in writing, (b) it is written in the service agreement with the rate, the way it is billed, and the statement that it is not covered by third-party payers, and (c) the client or representative has signed the agreement (CR-06).

Before a caregiver drives any client, HR verifies and records that the driver holds a valid driver's license, has an acceptable driving record, and, if using a personal vehicle, holds current auto insurance. The administrator confirms that the agency's insurance (including non-owned auto coverage) applies.

The agency obtains the client's consent to transport, including the destination, and notes any mobility needs. Caregivers use seat belts, child and wheelchair restraints where required, and do not transport more people than the vehicle can carry safely.
Drivers do not use hand-held phones while driving, do not drive impaired or fatigued, and do not leave the client unattended in a vehicle.
If an accident or injury occurs during transport, the driver calls 911 if needed, then the on-call line, and the event is reported as an incident under ENV-09.

Caregivers who use their own vehicles for non-client agency business are not covered by this policy for client transport. Client transport using a personal vehicle is not permitted unless the conditions above are met.
The administrator reviews private-pay transport use, insurance and driver records at least annually and during Quality Assurance reviews (ADM-08).

responsibilities.duty: Approves any private-pay transport, maintains insurance and reviews driver records.
Explains the limit on transport and discloses private-pay costs in the service agreement.
Keeps transport out of Medicaid billing and schedules private-pay transport only if approved.
Declines unauthorized transport, follows driving safety rules and reports accidents.

documentation: Service agreement showing any private-pay transport, rate and disclosure of costs not covered
Driver license, driving record and insurance verification
Insurance certificate showing non-owned auto coverage
Client consent to transport
Referral notes for community transportation
Incident reports for accidents

policies.title: Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation Prevention and Reporting
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors, supervisors and volunteers
policies.purpose: To keep clients free from abuse, neglect, involuntary seclusion and exploitation, and to make sure every suspected case is reported immediately to the proper authority and acted on.
policies.policy: Clients have the right to be free from abuse, neglect, involuntary seclusion and exploitation (COMAR 10.07.05.16). [AGENCY NAME] does not tolerate any of these by staff, family or others. Any employee or contractor who suspects that a client has been abused, neglected, has neglected themselves, or has been exploited reports it immediately to the local department of social services, as required by COMAR 07.02.16 and referenced in COMAR 10.09.84.05. Where a child is involved, the report goes to Child Protective Services at the local department of social services. For Medicaid clients, the incident is also reported within 24 hours of knowledge under ENV-09. Staff are trained on prevention and reporting (COMAR 10.07.05.11). Retaliation against anyone who reports in good faith is prohibited. The OHCQ complaint hotline is 800-492-6005.

definitions.definition: Physical, sexual, verbal or emotional harm, including hitting, rough handling, threats, humiliation, unreasonable restraint, and sexual contact of any kind.
Failure to provide goods or services needed for a client's health and safety, including leaving a client unattended who needs help, withholding food, hygiene, medication or care.
Failure of a client to meet their own basic needs, resulting in a risk to health or safety.
Improper use of a client's money, property or resources, including theft, coercion, misuse of accounts, pressure for gifts or loans.
Separation of a client from others against the client's will or confinement to an area.
The county or Baltimore City agency that receives and investigates reports under Adult Protective Services and Child Protective Services.

procedures: Prevention: [AGENCY NAME] screens all staff before referral under PER-03, orients them on this policy, and retrains them at least annually. Training content covers recognizing signs of abuse, neglect, self-neglect and exploitation, reporting duties, protection from retaliation, and boundaries (PER-09).

Clients receive written information on their right to be free from abuse, neglect, involuntary seclusion and exploitation, the agency complaint process, the OHCQ hotline (800-492-6005) and how to reach Adult or Child Protective Services at admission (CR-01 and CR-02).

Any staff member who sees, hears about or suspects abuse, neglect, self-neglect or exploitation immediately protects the client from immediate danger and calls 911 if anyone is in immediate danger or a crime is in progress.

The staff member reports the concern immediately to the local department of social services (Adult Protective Services, or Child Protective Services for a minor), by telephone, and does not wait for the agency's own review. The staff member then notifies the supervisor or on-call RN, [PHONE], as soon as possible. A staff member may make the report directly; telling a supervisor does not replace the staff member's own duty to report.

The supervisor or on-call RN confirms that the report to the local department of social services was made. If it was not, the supervisor makes it immediately and records the name of the person spoken to, date and time.

The supervisor notifies the administrator the same day. The administrator ensures the client is safe, and if the suspected person is a staff member, immediately removes that person from contact with the client pending review.
For Medicaid clients, the administrator makes the incident report within 24 hours of the agency's knowledge and submits the written report within 7 calendar days on the Department's form (ENV-09).

The agency notifies the client's representative, the case manager or supports planner and the physician as appropriate, unless the representative is the suspected person, in which case notice is made to the local department of social services and law enforcement as directed by them.

Where required, the agency also notifies OHCQ and law enforcement. Clients may also report to OHCQ at 800-492-6005. The administrator is the agency contact for any outside investigation and staff cooperate fully.

Staff do not investigate by interrogating the client or accused person, do not confront the suspected person, and preserve evidence, records and schedules. The administrator conducts only the internal fact-finding that does not interfere with the investigation by authorities.

The agency documents the report, the person receiving the report, date and time, actions taken and outcome, in an incident file that is separate from the caregiver's personnel record and with access limited as needed to protect the client.

When an employee is found to have abused, neglected or exploited a client, the administrator terminates the assignment, takes disciplinary action up to termination, and makes any required report to licensing or certification boards and the nurse aide or employee registry as covered in PER-03.
Retaliation against a client or staff member who reports in good faith is prohibited. The administrator investigates any claim of retaliation and takes corrective action.
The administrator reviews all reports quarterly for trends and adds corrective actions to the Quality Assurance review (ADM-08).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures reports are made, protects clients, removes suspected staff, files reports and prevents retaliation.
Confirms reporting, assesses the client, arranges safety measures and documents.
Report suspected abuse, neglect, self-neglect or exploitation immediately to the local department of social services and to the supervisor, and cooperate with investigators.
Provides orientation and annual training and keeps attendance records.

documentation: Written record of each report: date, time, person receiving it, details, actions and outcome
Incident report and Department form where applicable
Staff training records on abuse and neglect
Client acknowledgement of rights and hotline information
Personnel actions and referrals
Quality Assurance review of trends

policies.title: Incident Reporting
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors, supervisors and the administrator
policies.purpose: To make sure incidents and complaints are reported, investigated and documented on time, that the right parties are notified, and that actions are taken to prevent recurrence.
policies.policy: Staff report every incident to the agency the same day. For clients receiving Medicaid personal assistance, [AGENCY NAME] reports incidents and complaints within 24 hours of the agency's knowledge and submits a written report within 7 calendar days on the Department's form (COMAR 10.09.84.05). Every investigation records the time, date, place, people involved, a full description, the disposition and the follow-up to prevent recurrence. If no investigation is done, the reason is documented (COMAR 10.07.05.09). The agency notifies the client or representative, the physician where needed, and licensing or law enforcement agencies when required. Suspected abuse, neglect, self-neglect or exploitation is also reported immediately to the local department of social services under ENV-08.

definitions.definition: Any unusual or unexpected event involving a client, staff member or visitor that affects or could affect health, safety, rights or property, including falls, injuries, emergency calls or hospitalization, deaths, medication errors, missing or unaccounted-for client, abuse, neglect or exploitation allegations, threats or violence, theft or property loss or damage, equipment failure, infection exposure, and a client's complaint about care.
The time at which any agency employee or contractor first learns of the incident or complaint.
The incident/complaint reporting form prescribed by the Maryland Department of Health for Community First Choice and CPAS providers.

procedures: A staff member who witnesses, learns of, or is involved in an incident gives immediate care or calls 911 as needed, makes the client safe, and then notifies the supervisor or on-call line, [PHONE], without delay and the same day at the latest.

The staff member completes the agency incident report before the end of the shift, with facts only: time, date, place, people involved, what happened, what was done, and who was notified. The staff member does not alter the client record to hide an event.

The supervisor or on-call RN reviews the report, assesses the client (or directs the caregiver to emergency care), and notifies the administrator immediately for any death, serious injury, hospitalization, abuse or neglect allegation, violence, or missing client; and by the next business day for all others.

The administrator decides within 24 hours whether the event involves a Medicaid client. If it does, the administrator reports the incident or complaint to the Department within 24 hours of the agency's knowledge, using the method the Department specifies, and records the date, time, method and person receiving it.
The administrator completes and submits the written report on the Department's form within 7 calendar days of the incident, and files a copy in the incident file.
Where abuse, neglect, self-neglect or exploitation is suspected, the administrator confirms that the report to the local department of social services was made immediately (ENV-08).

The agency notifies the client or representative of the incident and what is being done, the physician where a change in condition or treatment is involved, OHCQ or other licensing authorities where required, and law enforcement for suspected crimes. Each notification is documented with date, time and the person notified.

The administrator or a designee who is not involved in the event investigates. The investigation records the time, date, place and people involved; a full description based on interviews, schedules and records; the disposition (substantiated, not substantiated, or unable to determine); and the follow-up to prevent recurrence.
If the administrator decides not to investigate, the administrator records the reason in the incident file, for example that the matter was referred to and is being investigated by another authority.

Complaints made by a client or representative are also handled under CR-02. A written complaint is handled promptly without disrupting services and the client is told the outcome. The OHCQ complaint hotline, 800-492-6005, is given to the client.
The agency gives OHCQ the investigation report immediately on request and provides a public summary on request, as permitted by law.

Follow-up actions, such as staff retraining, a plan-of-care update, equipment repair, or discipline, are assigned an owner and a due date, and the administrator verifies that they were completed. The RN updates the service plan when the event shows a change in need (PC-02, PC-09).
The administrator keeps an incident log and reviews it at least quarterly for trends. Findings go to the Quality Assurance review and the governing authority (ADM-01, ADM-08).
Incident files are kept with the quality and compliance records for at least 6 years from the date of service or incident, whichever is later, and are protected as confidential under CR-03.
Staff are trained on this policy at orientation and annually. No staff member is penalized for reporting an incident in good faith.

responsibilities.duty: Makes the 24-hour report and 7-day written report, directs investigations, ensures notifications and follow-up and reviews trends.
Assesses the client, takes immediate action, notifies the physician and representative and documents.
Report incidents promptly, complete the incident report and cooperate with investigation.
Maintains the incident log and reports trends.

documentation: Incident report
Date, time and recipient of the 24-hour report
Written report on the Department's form within 7 calendar days
Investigation report with time, date, place, people, description, disposition and follow-up
Reasons for any decision not to investigate
Notifications to client or representative, physician, licensing and law enforcement
Incident log and trend review

policies.title: Client Rights and Responsibilities
policies.applies_to: All clients and their representatives; all staff
policies.purpose: To make sure every client knows and can use his or her rights, understands his or her responsibilities, and is treated with dignity and respect.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] has a written client rights and responsibilities policy that is available to every client (COMAR 10.07.05.16). Each client receives a written statement of rights at or before admission. Rights include dignity and respect; participation in developing the plan of care; the right to refuse treatment; privacy; confidentiality; freedom from abuse, neglect, involuntary seclusion and exploitation; and the right to complain without retaliation and receive a prompt response. The agency also provides the caregiver's name, the care supervisor's name and contact, and the 24/7 phone number; discloses subcontractual relationships; and provides a cost estimate and a statement of costs not covered by third parties, with itemized bills on request. Clients are given access to complaint procedures for OHCQ and for Adult or Child Protective Services. Rights are exercised by the client or, as permitted, by a recognized representative (COMAR 10.07.05.13). For Medicaid-funded home and community-based services, these rights are applied consistent with 42 CFR 441.301(c).

definitions.definition: A guardian of the person or property, a person acting under an advance directive, a surrogate decision maker, an agent under a power of attorney, a representative payee, or a person the competent client has designated in writing.
The RN or other qualified person responsible for supervising the client's care and caregiver.
