Any adverse action, such as reduced service, changed caregiver, threats, or discharge, taken because a client or representative exercised a right or made a complaint.

procedures: At or before the start of services, the intake coordinator or RN reviews the written Client Rights and Responsibilities with the client or representative, in a language and format the client understands (CR-05), and answers questions.
The agency gives the client a copy and obtains a signed and dated acknowledgement for the record. If the client cannot or will not sign, the staff member writes this and the reason.

At the same time the agency gives the client in writing: the caregiver's name; the care supervisor's name and phone number; the 24/7 phone number, [PHONE]; the written on-call procedures; and disclosure of any subcontractual relationship under which services will be provided (PER-10).
The agency gives the client a cost estimate and a statement of costs not covered by third-party payers before services begin, and provides itemized bills on request (CR-06).

The agency gives the client written information on how to complain to [AGENCY NAME] (CR-02) and to OHCQ (hotline 800-492-6005, office 410-402-8040), and how to contact Adult Protective Services or Child Protective Services at the local department of social services. Contact numbers are in the client's service agreement and in the home folder.

The agency gives the client written information on advance directives, asks whether the client has one, and records the answer and places a copy in the record if provided. Care is not conditioned on having or not having an advance directive (IC-04).

The agency identifies any client representative, records the representative's name, and keeps the authorizing document in the record. The agency does not honor a representative who exceeds the authority granted. A competent client keeps all rights not delegated.

The RN involves the client in developing and changing the plan of care. The client may refuse a treatment or service, and the agency honors the refusal and documents it, after explaining the risks and benefits. Waivers of skilled services are honored when documented under IC-03.
Informed consent information given to the client includes the purpose of the service, alternatives, side effects and benefits, cost, and the right to withdraw consent at any time (IC-01, IC-02).

Clients may accept or reject any referred caregiver without retaliation. A client who asks for a different caregiver is accommodated where practicable and the request is recorded. Medicaid participants are also directed to their case manager or supports planner.

Staff protect client privacy and confidentiality in the home, in documentation and in conversation, in line with CR-03. Staff treat clients with dignity, address them by their preferred name, and respect cultural and personal preferences.

Clients are told of their responsibilities: giving accurate and complete information; telling the agency of changes in health, hospitalization, address, insurance or Medicaid status; being at home or giving notice for a missed or changed visit; providing a reasonably safe environment; treating staff with respect; following the plan or telling the agency of disagreement; and paying for non-covered services as agreed in the service agreement.
A client who complains or exercises a right is not retaliated against. Any report of retaliation is investigated by the administrator under CR-02 and ENV-09.
All staff are trained on client rights at orientation and annually (PER-06). Staff may not ask clients to waive these rights.
The administrator reviews the rights statement at least annually and updates it when regulations change. The governing authority reviews it with the other policies (ADM-01).
The RN or supervisor reviews rights with the client again at the annual reassessment and any time the client or representative asks, and documents it.

responsibilities.duty: Maintains the rights statement, ensures distribution, investigates alleged violations and prevents retaliation.
Reviews rights with the client at admission, obtains the signed acknowledgement, and gives the caregiver and supervisor information and cost documents.
Respect the client's rights, protect privacy and dignity, and report concerns.
Exercises rights and meets the responsibilities listed.

documentation: Written client rights and responsibilities
Signed and dated acknowledgement
Written caregiver, supervisor and 24/7 contact information
Cost estimate and statement of non-covered costs
Advance directive information and any copy
Representative's name or authorizing document
Records of refusals, caregiver requests and complaints
Staff training records

policies.title: Grievances and Complaints
policies.applies_to: All clients and client representatives; all employees, contractors and subcontract staff of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To give every client and representative a clear, safe way to raise a complaint or grievance, and to make sure [AGENCY NAME] investigates each one promptly, documents it, reports it where required, and uses the findings to prevent a repeat. The policy meets the Maryland complaint-process requirements for Residential Service Agencies (COMAR 10.07.05.09), the client-rights requirements (COMAR 10.07.05.16) and the Medicaid incident and complaint reporting requirements (COMAR 10.09.84.05).
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains a written internal complaint process. Each client or representative is told about it at admission and receives it in writing. Complaints may be made orally or in writing, by the client, a representative, a family member or anyone acting for the client. [AGENCY NAME] handles written complaints promptly and keeps services going while the complaint is reviewed. No client, representative or employee is retaliated against for making a complaint, and clients keep the right to accept or reject any referred caregiver without retaliation. Every client receives the OHCQ complaint hotline, 800-492-6005, and information on how to contact Adult or Child Protective Services through the local department of social services. Using the agency's process is never a condition of contacting OHCQ or protective services. For every complaint investigated, a written investigation report records the time, date and place of the events, the people involved, a full description, the disposition, and the follow-up taken to prevent recurrence. If [AGENCY NAME] decides not to investigate a complaint, the reason is documented. Investigation reports are given to OHCQ immediately on request, and a public summary is available on request as permitted by law. For Medicaid (CFC/CPAS) participants, complaints and incidents are reported to the Department within 24 hours of the agency's knowledge, with a written report on the Department's form within 7 calendar days.

definitions.definition: Any expression of dissatisfaction or concern about the agency, its services, its caregivers or supervisors, billing, or a client's rights, whether oral or written and whether or not the person calls it a complaint.
A complaint that is not resolved at the point of first contact and so goes through the formal investigation and written-response steps of this policy.
The person designated by the Administrator to receive, log, assign and track complaints. Unless otherwise designated, this is [ADMINISTRATOR NAME].
The finding on the complaint (for example substantiated, partly substantiated or not substantiated) and the action taken.

procedures: At admission, the intake staff member gives the client or representative the written Complaint Procedure and the OHCQ complaint hotline number (800-492-6005), explains them verbally, and records on the Client Rights Acknowledgement that this was done. The Complaint Procedure also gives the agency's 24/7 number [PHONE] and the name and contact of the care supervisor.

The written notice also tells the client how to reach Adult Protective Services or Child Protective Services through the local department of social services, states that no one will be retaliated against, and states that the client may contact OHCQ at any time without first using the agency's process.

Any employee who receives a complaint, in person, by phone, by text, by email or in writing, writes it on the Complaint Intake Form the same day. The form records the date and time received, the complainant, the client, the people involved and what was said. No employee may discourage, screen out or delay a complaint.

The employee forwards the Intake Form to the Complaint Coordinator within one business day. If the complaint alleges abuse, neglect, exploitation or immediate danger, the employee notifies the Complaint Coordinator or on-call RN immediately.

The Complaint Coordinator assigns a complaint number, enters it in the Complaint Log, and sorts it as (a) a service or billing concern, (b) a possible rights violation, or (c) suspected abuse, neglect, self-neglect or exploitation.

For category (c), the Coordinator immediately starts the reporting steps in ENV-08 (notice to the local department of social services and, where required, law enforcement and OHCQ). The Coordinator also takes any needed steps to protect the client, such as removing the caregiver from the case pending review. Protective action is taken before the investigation is complete.

The Coordinator acknowledges a written complaint to the complainant, in writing, within 2 business days. If the complaint was oral and the client wants to remain anonymous or does not want a written follow-up, this is documented.

For a Medicaid participant, the Administrator decides within the same business day whether the matter is a reportable complaint or incident. If it is, the Administrator reports it to the Department within 24 hours of the agency's knowledge, and the written report on the Department's form is submitted within 7 calendar days. The date and time of knowledge, the 24-hour report and the 7-day report are each recorded in the Complaint Log.

The Coordinator, or an RN or manager assigned by the Administrator, investigates. The investigator is not someone involved in the events complained of. The investigator interviews the complainant, the client, the caregiver and any witnesses, and reviews the service plan, visit and timekeeping records, and other relevant documents.

Services continue during the investigation without disruption. If the client does not want the involved caregiver, the Coordinator arranges a replacement under PC-07 and documents the change. The client may accept or reject any caregiver without retaliation.

The investigation is completed and the written report issued within 14 calendar days of receipt. If more time is needed, the Coordinator documents the reason and tells the complainant in writing of the new target date.

The Investigation Report states: the time, date and place of the events; the people involved; a full description of the events and complaint; the evidence reviewed; the disposition; and the follow-up action to prevent recurrence (for example retraining, discipline, a change in the service plan, or a change in procedure).

If the agency decides not to investigate (for example, the complaint is withdrawn, is outside the agency's control, or is a duplicate of one already resolved), the Administrator documents the specific reason in the file and tells the complainant.

The Coordinator notifies the client or representative of the findings and outcome in writing. The Coordinator also notifies the client's physician when the matter affects the client's care or health, and notifies licensing authorities (OHCQ) or law enforcement when required by law.

Corrective actions are assigned to a named person with a due date, and the Coordinator verifies completion and records it on the report. Personnel actions are carried out under PER-09 and recorded in the personnel file.

The Coordinator gives the Investigation Report to OHCQ immediately on request. When a member of the public requests a summary, the Coordinator provides it as permitted by law, with client and employee identifiers removed.
The Complaint Log is reviewed quarterly by the QA committee under ADM-08 for trends by caregiver, supervisor, service type and cause. Results and system changes are recorded in the QA minutes.

responsibilities.duty: Owns the complaint process; decides Medicaid reportability; submits 24-hour and 7-day reports; ensures corrective actions are completed; reports to OHCQ and other authorities.
Receives and logs all complaints, assigns the investigator, tracks deadlines, sends written acknowledgements and outcomes, and maintains the Complaint Log and files.
Investigates clinical and service complaints, takes protective action for clients, and notifies physicians when care is affected.
Accept every complaint without discouraging it, record it the same day, forward it within one business day, and never retaliate.
May complain orally or in writing to the agency, to OHCQ (800-492-6005) or to protective services at any time.

documentation: Signed Client Rights Acknowledgement showing the complaint procedure and OHCQ hotline were given
Complaint Intake Form
Complaint Log (number, dates received, acknowledged, closed, and Medicaid 24-hour and 7-day report dates)
Investigation Report (time, date, place, people involved, description, disposition, prevention follow-up) or documented reason for not investigating
Written acknowledgement and outcome letters to the complainant
Copies of reports to the Department, OHCQ, the local department of social services and law enforcement
Corrective action records and QA committee minutes

policies.title: Privacy, Confidentiality and HIPAA
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors, subcontract staff, volunteers and students of [AGENCY NAME]; all client information in any form
policies.purpose: To protect the privacy and confidentiality of client information, to release it only as the law allows, and to respond correctly to any breach. The policy follows the Maryland records and confidentiality requirements (COMAR 10.07.05.15), the required training content on ethics and confidentiality (COMAR 10.07.05.11) and the HIPAA Privacy Rule (45 CFR 164.502 and 164.530).
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] treats all client records and information as confidential. Information is released only with the client's written consent or as permitted by Maryland Health-General Title 4, Subtitle 3 and the HIPAA Privacy Rule. [AGENCY NAME] uses and discloses protected health information only as 45 CFR 164.502 allows, and limits uses and disclosures to the minimum necessary except where the rule says otherwise. It gives each client a Notice of Privacy Practices at admission and obtains a written acknowledgement. It safeguards records against loss, destruction and unauthorized use. All staff are trained on confidentiality at orientation and each year, as part of the required training on ethics and confidentiality. The agency has a designated Privacy Officer, and the administrative requirements of 45 CFR 164.530 (training, safeguards, complaints, sanctions, mitigation, no retaliation and documentation) are carried out under this policy. Breaches of unsecured protected health information are investigated and reported under the HIPAA Breach Notification Rule.

definitions.definition: Individually identifiable information about a client's health, care or payment for care, in any form (paper, electronic, spoken), including name, address, diagnosis, schedule and photographs.
The least amount of PHI needed to accomplish the purpose of a use or disclosure.

An acquisition, access, use or disclosure of unsecured PHI not permitted by the Privacy Rule that compromises its privacy or security, unless a documented risk assessment shows a low probability that the PHI was compromised.
The person responsible for the privacy program and for receiving privacy complaints: [PRIVACY OFFICER NAME], [PHONE].

procedures: The Administrator designates a Privacy Officer in writing and the name and contact information are in the Notice of Privacy Practices.

At admission, the intake staff member gives the client or representative the Notice of Privacy Practices, explains it in plain language (using interpreter services where needed under CR-05), and obtains a signed acknowledgement. If the client will not sign, staff document the date and the good-faith effort.

All new staff sign a Confidentiality Agreement before any client contact. Training on confidentiality, HIPAA, safeguarding information and breach reporting is given at orientation (PER-06) and refreshed annually. Attendance is recorded in the personnel file.
Staff access client information only when needed for their job duties. Supervisors give access to the client record by role and remove access on the day an employee or contractor separates.

Staff do not discuss clients in public places, by personal social media, in group texts or with other clients. Staff do not take or post photographs or video of clients. Caregivers do not keep client information on personal devices unless the device is approved and secured by the Administrator.

Before releasing any information, the Privacy Officer or designee confirms the request is (a) signed by the client or representative with a valid written authorization, or (b) permitted without authorization by Health-General Title 4, Subtitle 3 or the Privacy Rule (for example treatment, payment, operations, or required reporting of abuse). Each release is logged with date, recipient, purpose and what was released.

Written authorizations state who may receive what information, for what purpose, and when the authorization expires, and tell the client that it can be revoked in writing. A representative's authority is verified under IC-04 before information is released to the representative.

Paper records are kept in locked cabinets in a locked office. Electronic records require unique user IDs, strong passwords, automatic log-off, encryption of laptops and portable media, and regular backups. Records are never left in vehicles or unattended in homes.

Caregiver visit notes and any papers left in the home contain only the information needed for care. Documents are returned to the office or shredded as directed; PHI is never thrown in the household trash.

Clients may request access to their record, an amendment, an accounting of disclosures, and restrictions on use. The Privacy Officer responds in writing within the time frames required by the Privacy Rule and documents each request and response.
Any employee who knows of or suspects an improper access, use, loss or disclosure of PHI reports it to the Privacy Officer immediately, and no later than the end of the same business day.

The Privacy Officer opens a breach file, takes immediate steps to contain the problem and retrieve the information, and completes a documented risk assessment (nature of the PHI, who received it, whether it was actually viewed, and how far the risk has been reduced).

If the assessment does not show a low probability of compromise, the agency treats the event as a reportable breach. It notifies each affected client or representative in writing without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 calendar days after discovery. It reports to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services as the Breach Notification Rule requires, and gives media notice where the rule requires it. Where other State law requires notice, the Administrator also makes that notice.
Where a breach also involves a Medicaid participant or a safety event, the Administrator decides whether it is an incident to be reported under REC-02 and ENV-09.

Employees who violate this policy are subject to sanctions up to termination, applied consistently and documented in the personnel file. No one is retaliated against for reporting a privacy concern or filing a privacy complaint.
Privacy complaints are handled under CR-02. The Privacy Officer reviews safeguards, access logs and breach files at least annually and reports to the QA committee (ADM-08).

Privacy and security policies, and records of training, authorizations, requests, disclosures and breach files, are kept for at least 6 years, as 45 CFR 164.530 and the Security Rule documentation provisions require, or longer when REC-01 requires.

responsibilities.duty: Designates the Privacy Officer, resources safeguards, approves sanctions and decides on external breach notices.
Runs the privacy program, trains staff, handles release requests and client rights requests, investigates and documents breaches, and maintains logs.
Give the Notice of Privacy Practices and obtain the acknowledgement at admission.
Coach caregivers on privacy in the home and in documentation; report suspected breaches immediately.
Protect client information, access it only as needed, and report any suspected breach the same day.

documentation: Signed Notice of Privacy Practices acknowledgement for each client
Signed staff Confidentiality Agreements
Training attendance records and content outlines
Signed authorizations for release and Release/Disclosure Log
Client requests for access, amendment or accounting, and responses
Breach file: report, risk assessment, notices sent, and agency actions
Sanction records and annual privacy and security review

policies.title: Client Property, Gifts and Financial Exploitation Prevention
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors and subcontract staff of [AGENCY NAME]; all clients and their property
policies.purpose: To protect clients' property and finances and to uphold the client right to be free from exploitation (COMAR 10.07.05.16), and to carry out the required training on prevention of abuse and neglect (COMAR 10.07.05.11).
policies.policy: Freedom from abuse, neglect, involuntary seclusion and exploitation is a client right. This is [AGENCY NAME]'s written policy on gifts, loans and client money. Employees and contractors may not accept gifts, money, loans or property from clients or their families. They may not ask for them, may not borrow from or lend to clients, and may not use client property, accounts, cards or vehicles for personal use. They do not handle a client's money except for an authorized errand as set out below. Employees may not serve as a client's agent, power of attorney, representative payee or health care agent, may not accept being named in a client's will or as a beneficiary, and may not be added to a client's bank account. The agency itself does not serve as a client's representative payee or agent. Suspected exploitation is reported immediately to the local department of social services, and to the Department within 24 hours where the client is a Medicaid participant. Actions taken by a representative payee or power of attorney are documented in the client record.

definitions.definition: Taking, misusing or obtaining a client's money, property, benefits or services through deception, undue influence, coercion or breach of trust.
Shopping or another task involving a client's money that is written into the service plan and signed by the client or representative.
A person or organization appointed by an agency such as the Social Security Administration to manage a client's benefits.
A legal document in which a client gives another person authority to act for the client in financial or other matters.

procedures: At admission, the intake staff member gives the client or representative a written explanation of this policy. It says that caregivers may not accept gifts or loans or handle money except as written in the service plan, and tells the client how to report a concern (CR-02).

During orientation (PER-06) and every year, all staff are trained on exploitation and financial exploitation, warning signs, the gift and loan rules, and the duty to report. Training is documented under C5 content on prevention of abuse and neglect. Each employee signs this policy.

A caregiver who is offered a gift, money or a loan politely declines and tells the supervisor the same day. The supervisor records the offer on a Gift Offer Report. If a client insists on a small token such as a card or a homemade item that cannot reasonably be refused, the supervisor decides whether to accept it on behalf of the agency, and records the decision.

Caregivers do not borrow, lend, sell or buy anything from a client. They do not take client belongings, do not use the client's phone, car, credit or debit card or online accounts, and do not obtain or keep PINs or passwords.

Shopping or other errands with client money are done only if the service plan authorizes them in writing. The plan names the task, the client's preferred stores and a spending limit of [DOLLAR LIMIT].

For an authorized errand, the caregiver counts the money with the client (or representative) before leaving, keeps it separate from personal funds, gets itemized receipts, returns the change and receipts to the client, and has the client sign the Errand Log. The caregiver never uses the client's card for any other purchase.

The caregiver does not handle large sums of cash, checks, jewelry or valuables, and does not sign for the client. If a client asks the caregiver to go to the bank, cash a check or pay bills, the caregiver declines and notifies the supervisor, who works out with the client or representative a safer arrangement.

At admission and each reassessment, the RN notes whether a POA, guardian or representative payee is in place, records the name and contact information, and obtains copies of the documents under IC-04. Where a representative acts on the client's behalf in a financial matter involving the agency (for example signing a service agreement or paying bills), the staff member records the date, the person acting and the action in the client record.

If a client reports that property is missing or damaged, the staff member who takes the report notes it on the Property Concern Form the same day and notifies the supervisor, who offers to help the client report it to the police and handles it under CR-02.

Staff who see signs of financial exploitation (unexplained withdrawals, new names on accounts, sudden changes to a will or POA, unpaid bills despite adequate funds, missing belongings, pressure by a third party) tell the supervisor at once.

If exploitation is suspected, by anyone including an employee or a family member, the supervisor or Administrator reports to the local department of social services immediately by phone and follows ENV-08 for written follow-up and any report to law enforcement or OHCQ. For a Medicaid participant, the Administrator also reports to the Department within 24 hours with the written report in 7 calendar days (REC-02).

The agency protects the client from further harm. This may include removing a caregiver from the case immediately, offering a different caregiver, and notifying the client's representative unless the representative is the suspected person.

The Administrator investigates employee involvement under CR-02. Substantiated exploitation by an employee leads to termination, and the agency makes any reports required to licensing, law enforcement and registries (PER-03).
The supervisor reviews Errand Logs, Gift Offer Reports and Property Concern Forms monthly. Patterns are reported to the QA committee (ADM-08).

responsibilities.duty: Enforces the policy, reports suspected exploitation, decides on discipline and removal of staff.
Writes errand authorizations into the service plan, reviews logs monthly, records representative/POA information, and responds to concerns.
Decline gifts and loans, follow errand procedures exactly, and report concerns the same day.
Explain the policy at admission and obtain signed acknowledgement.

documentation: Signed client acknowledgement of the gifts, loans and money policy
Employee signed policy acknowledgement and training records
Service plan errand authorization and spending limit
Errand Log with receipts and client signature
Gift Offer Report and Property Concern Form
Records of representative payee, POA and representative actions in the client record
Reports to the local department of social services, the Department and OHCQ, and investigation files

policies.title: Nondiscrimination and Language Access
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors and subcontract staff of [AGENCY NAME]; all applicants, clients, representatives and job applicants
policies.purpose: To make sure services are provided and clients are treated without discrimination, and that people with limited English proficiency or disabilities can understand and take part in their care. This supports the client right to dignity, participation in the care plan and freedom from abuse and exploitation (COMAR 10.07.05.16), and meets Title VI of the Civil Rights Act (42 U.S.C. 2000d), the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) and 45 CFR Part 92.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not discriminate on the basis of race, color, national origin, disability, age or sex in admission, services, assignment of caregivers, discharge or employment. This includes discrimination on the basis of limited English proficiency. Under 45 CFR Part 92, sex includes the characteristics the rule covers. The agency provides qualified interpreter and translation services free of charge to clients and representatives who have limited English proficiency or who are deaf or hard of hearing, and provides auxiliary aids and reasonable accommodations at no charge to people with disabilities. Friends and family members are not used as interpreters unless the client asks, and minors are never used except in an emergency. A Notice of Nondiscrimination and notice of language assistance services are included in every client packet and posted in the office. Admission decisions are based on the agency's ability to meet the client's needs safely (ADM-05), and not on any protected characteristic. A client's right to accept or reject any referred caregiver without retaliation is respected. Clients who believe they have been discriminated against may file a grievance under CR-02 or complain directly to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office for Civil Rights.

definitions.definition: A limited ability to read, speak, write or understand English well enough to take part effectively in care.
A person who is competent in both languages, adheres to interpreter ethics, including confidentiality and impartiality, and can interpret accurately, effectively and impartially.
Aids that make communication effective for people with disabilities, such as sign language interpreters, large print, Braille, captioning and accessible electronic formats.
A change in a policy, practice or procedure that gives a person with a disability equal access to services, unless it would fundamentally alter the service or impose an undue burden.

procedures: The Administrator designates a Nondiscrimination Coordinator ([COORDINATOR NAME], [PHONE]) in writing. The Coordinator receives discrimination grievances and oversees language access and accommodation requests.

At first contact and at intake, staff ask the client or representative, 'What language do you prefer to speak and read in, and do you need any help to communicate or take part?' The answers are recorded in the client record and the service plan.

If the client or representative has limited English proficiency, intake staff arrange a qualified interpreter, in person, by phone or by video, at no charge, for the assessment, the service plan review, consent discussions and any time the client asks. The interpreter's name or service ID is recorded each time.

Staff do not require or pressure a client to bring their own interpreter. A client may choose to use a family member or friend. If so, staff record that the client was offered a free qualified interpreter and declined. A minor child is never used as an interpreter, except in a real emergency until a qualified interpreter is available.

Key documents (the rights statement, Notice of Privacy Practices, service agreement, consent forms, complaint procedure and the OHCQ hotline number) are provided in the client's preferred language where available. If not, a qualified translator or interpreter reads them aloud and the staff member records that this was done.

For clients who are deaf, hard of hearing, blind or have low vision or cognitive or speech disabilities, staff provide the auxiliary aid or service the client chooses where possible, for example a sign language interpreter, large print, reading documents aloud or extra time. These are provided at no charge.

Reasonable accommodation requests from clients and applicants are written on the Accommodation Request Form, decided by the Nondiscrimination Coordinator within 5 business days, and recorded with the reason for any denial and the alternative offered. Services continue meanwhile.

The Notice of Nondiscrimination, which states the agency's policy, how to get language assistance and how to file a grievance with the agency and with the HHS Office for Civil Rights, is included in the client packet, on the agency website and posted in the office.

When matching caregivers to clients, the scheduler considers client language, culture and stated preferences. A client's request for a caregiver of a particular gender for personal care is honored where possible as a privacy preference. Staff may not refuse an assignment because of the client's race, color, national origin, disability, age, sex or similar characteristic, and may not make discriminatory remarks.

Intake staff apply admission criteria consistently (ADM-05). If an applicant is declined, the reason is documented as a service or safety reason, for example a service not offered or no staff available, and never as a protected characteristic. A written referral to other providers is offered.

All staff are trained on nondiscrimination, cultural humility, working with interpreters and disability etiquette at orientation and annually (PER-06). Staff who discriminate are disciplined under PER-09.

Discrimination complaints are handled under CR-02. The Nondiscrimination Coordinator investigates, responds in writing and informs the complainant of the right to complain to the HHS Office for Civil Rights. No one is retaliated against for complaining.

The Nondiscrimination Coordinator keeps a log of interpreter use and accommodation requests, and reports annually to the QA committee (ADM-08) on language needs in the service area, the adequacy of services and complaints.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures compliance, funds interpreter and translation services, and enforces discipline.
Receives grievances and accommodation requests, maintains the logs, and keeps notices current.
Ask language and communication needs at intake, arrange interpreters and aids, and record them.
Match caregivers with language and preference considerations; never assign or refuse on a discriminatory basis.
Treat all clients with dignity and respect; use interpreters; report discrimination concerns.

documentation: Language and communication needs recorded in the client record and service plan
Interpreter log (date, language, interpreter name or service ID, purpose)
Record of declined interpreter services
Accommodation Request Forms and decisions
Notice of Nondiscrimination in client packet (copy of packet on file)
Training records on nondiscrimination and language access
Discrimination grievance files under CR-02 and annual QA report

policies.title: Service Agreement, Cost Estimate, Rates and Billing Disclosure
policies.applies_to: All clients and representatives; intake, billing and supervisory staff of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure every client and representative receives a written service agreement, a clear cost estimate and full disclosure of charges, caregiver and supervisor identity, subcontract relationships and the 24/7 number before and during service. The policy meets the disclosures required by COMAR 10.07.05.16, and the Medicaid payment rules in COMAR 10.09.84.24 and Medicaid rates in Transmittal PT 03-25.
policies.policy: Before services start, [AGENCY NAME] gives the client or representative a written service agreement and a written cost estimate. These state the services, the hours and frequency, the rate and the expected cost. The cost estimate is accompanied by a statement of any costs that are not covered by third-party payers such as Medicaid or insurance. Itemized bills are provided on request. The client is told the caregiver's name, the name and contact information of the care supervisor, and the agency's 24/7 telephone number. Any subcontractual relationship used to provide the client's services is disclosed in writing. For Medicaid personal assistance (CFC and CPAS), [AGENCY NAME] bills only services preauthorized in the plan of service, delivered consistent with it and within the provider agreement. It documents time with the Department-approved telephonic timekeeping system, and is paid the lesser of its usual and customary charge to the general public or the Department's fee schedule rate. Therefore the agency's private-pay rate is not set below the Medicaid rate, because a lower rate to the general public would reduce what Medicaid pays. The Medicaid rates are posted and available to clients.

definitions.definition: A written statement given before service starts of the services, rates, expected charges and who pays.
The rate the agency charges the general public for the same service.
The rate the Department publishes for a service code. The Medicaid fee schedule rates for personal assistance are in Transmittal PT 03-25 (effective July 1, 2024).
A 15-minute period of billable personal assistance. Services up to 12 hours per day are paid in 15-minute units, and a daily rate applies above 12 hours.

procedures: Before the first visit, the intake staff member prepares the Service Agreement and the Cost Estimate for the client or representative, listing the services, the planned hours per week, the rate per hour or unit, the estimated weekly and monthly charge, and who will be billed (client, Medicaid, insurance or other payer).

The Cost Estimate includes a separate written statement of any costs not covered by third-party payers. For a private-pay client this states that all charges are the client's responsibility. For a Medicaid participant, it lists any services the agency may provide that are outside the plan of service and therefore not covered, and any other cost the client would owe.

The staff member reviews the documents aloud with the client or representative, using an interpreter where needed (CR-05), and answers questions. The client or representative signs and dates the Service Agreement, and a copy is given to the client at that time.

The Service Agreement and a Client Information Sheet give: the caregiver's name; the name, title and phone number of the care supervisor; the agency's 24/7 phone number [PHONE]; the OHCQ complaint hotline (800-492-6005); and the process for complaints (CR-02). When the caregiver or supervisor changes, the client is told and the sheet is updated.

The Service Agreement discloses in writing any subcontractual relationship used to deliver the client's services, naming the subcontract agency or contractor and what it provides (PER-10). The client is told before a subcontract worker is assigned.

The Administrator sets the agency's private-pay rate schedule in writing and reviews it at least annually. No private-pay rate for personal assistance is set below the current Medicaid rate for the same service, so that the lesser-of rule does not lower Medicaid payment. Any discounted rate is approved in writing by the Administrator after a check against this rule.

The Medicaid personal assistance rates are posted in the office and provided to any client on request. They are, as of PT 03-25 (effective July 1, 2024): $6.3962 per 15-minute unit ($25.58 per hour) for W5519 (CFC) and W5527 (CPAS); $4.2597 per 15 minutes for shared attendant services (W5521/W5528); and a daily rate of $329.84 for more than 12 hours per day (W5532). The billing manager confirms the rates against the Department's current fee schedule each July 1, since the Department publishes the schedule at least annually and rates may increase 3% each July 1 subject to the State budget, and updates the posting.

For Medicaid participants, the agency verifies Medicaid eligibility at the start of each month of service, and bills only services preauthorized in the plan of service. It does not bill for time not worked, not documented in the timekeeping system, or not consistent with the plan (ADM-07, PC-08).

Medicaid billing is based on time recorded through the Department-approved telephonic timekeeping system (PC-08). The billing manager reconciles recorded time to claims before each submission, and does not bill unauthorized hours, or alter timekeeping data.

The agency does not suspend, terminate, increase or reduce Medicaid services without Department authorization and consultation with the participant. The supervisor does not change hours or rates for a Medicaid participant on the agency's own authority (PC-10, PC-11).

Any change in the agency's rates, minimum hours or charges for private-pay clients is given to the client in writing at least 30 days before it takes effect, with a revised Cost Estimate for the client or representative to sign. A client who does not agree may end services without penalty and be helped to transfer (PC-10).

On request, the billing manager gives the client an itemized bill showing dates of service, hours or units, rate and total, within 10 business days. Billing questions are answered by the billing manager at [PHONE]. A billing complaint is handled under CR-02.

Billing errors or overpayments found by staff, clients or auditors are corrected promptly, with credits or refunds to the client and repayment to the payer as required, and are documented. The Administrator reports the matter to the compliance program (ADM-12).
Service agreements, cost estimates, rate schedules and billing records are kept in the client record and billing file under REC-01 for the required retention periods.

responsibilities.duty: Sets and approves rates (private-pay rate not below Medicaid), approves disclosures and ensures compliance with the lesser-of rule.
Prepare and review the Service Agreement and Cost Estimate and obtain signatures before service starts.
Posts and updates Medicaid rates, reconciles timekeeping to claims, verifies monthly eligibility, issues itemized bills and corrects errors.
Tell the client the caregiver and supervisor names and contact details, and keep them current.
Review and sign the agreement, and raise questions about charges.

documentation: Signed Service Agreement and Cost Estimate, with the statement of costs not covered by third parties
Client Information Sheet (caregiver name, supervisor name and contact, 24/7 phone, OHCQ hotline)
Written disclosure of subcontract relationships
Rate schedule (private-pay and Medicaid), with annual review and approvals
Posted Medicaid rate notice per PT 03-25 and later fee schedules
Monthly Medicaid eligibility verification records
Itemized bills issued, billing reconciliation to timekeeping data, and error and refund records

policies.title: Client Records and Retention
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors and subcontract staff of [AGENCY NAME] who create, use or store client records, in paper or electronic form
policies.purpose: To make sure complete, accurate and confidential client records are kept, protected and retained for the required periods, and are handled correctly if a client is discharged or the agency closes. The policy meets COMAR 10.07.05.15 (maintenance of records), the Medicaid documentation retention requirement of COMAR 10.09.84.05 and the HIPAA Security Rule documentation requirement of 45 CFR 164.316.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps a record for every client. Client records are kept for 5 years after discharge. For a minor, the record is kept until the client reaches age 21 or for 5 years after the record is made, whichever is later. Medicaid service documentation, including dates and hours of service, is kept for 6 years from the date of service. Where the two periods differ for the same record, the agency uses the longer period. A record of a discharged client is completed within 30 days of discharge. Records are confidential and are released only with written consent or as permitted by Health-General Title 4, Subtitle 3, under CR-03. Records are safeguarded against loss, destruction and unauthorized use. If the agency closes, records are returned to the client or representative or retained as required. Written security policies and procedures under the HIPAA Security Rule are retained for 6 years, in line with 45 CFR 164.316.

definitions.definition: All documents, paper or electronic, about a client's referral, assessment, service plan, services delivered, supervision, incidents, consents, communications and discharge.
Records showing dates, times and hours of services delivered, including visit notes and telephonic timekeeping and claims data.
The date on which the agency's services to the client end (PC-10).
The minimum time a record must be kept before it can be destroyed.

procedures: The agency opens one record for each client at admission (ADM-05). It contains at least: referral and intake information; the pre-acceptance assessment (ADM-06); the RN assessment and service plan (PC-02); signed consents, rights acknowledgements and the Service Agreement (CR-06); advance directive information (IC-04); the privacy acknowledgement (CR-03); visit and service documentation; supervisory visit notes; incident and complaint reports; and physician or case-manager communications.

Every entry is legible, dated, timed where relevant, and signed or electronically authenticated with the name and title of the person making it. Entries are made at or near the time of service and are never backdated. Corrections are made by a single line and initialed, or by a dated electronic addendum; originals are never erased or destroyed.

Caregivers turn in visit documentation to the office on the schedule set by the supervisor, at least weekly. The supervisor checks that the documentation matches the plan and the timekeeping data, and returns incomplete notes for correction.

Paper records are kept in locked cabinets in a locked area accessible only to authorized staff. Electronic records are kept in a system with unique user IDs, role-based access, audit logs, encryption and regular backup, stored in a secure location (CR-03). No records are left unattended in a vehicle or home.
Records leave the office only when needed for care or an audit. A sign-out log is kept, and records are returned the same day.

Records are released only with the client's or representative's written consent or as permitted by Health-General Title 4, Subtitle 3. Requests are sent to the Privacy Officer, who checks authority and logs each release (CR-03). Records are made available to OHCQ, the Department and its auditors when they request them in an inspection, review or audit.

When services end, the supervisor notifies the records clerk of the discharge date. Within 30 days of discharge, the RN or supervisor completes the record, including the discharge summary or transfer information (PC-10), final visit notes, missing signatures and corrections. The clerk checks the record against the Closed Record Checklist and signs the completion date.

The records clerk sets the destruction date for each record at closing as follows: for an adult, the later of 5 years after discharge and 6 years after the last date of service documented; for a minor, the later of age 21, 5 years after the record was made, and the Medicaid 6-year period. If the agency is aware of an audit, investigation, claim or litigation, the record is held until the Administrator releases it in writing.

Closed records are stored in a secure storage area, indexed by client and destruction date, and retrieval is logged. Electronic closed records are kept with the same safeguards and remain readable for the whole retention period (including when software or systems change).

On or after the destruction date, and with the Administrator's written approval, the clerk destroys records so that they cannot be read or rebuilt: paper by cross-cut shredding or a certified shredding vendor, and electronic media by secure wiping or physical destruction. A Destruction Log records the client ID, date, method and person responsible. The agency keeps a list of destroyed records, not their contents.
Billing, claims and timekeeping data for Medicaid services are kept for 6 years from the date of service in the billing file, and are linked to the client record (ADM-07).

Written security and privacy policies, risk analyses, training records and related documents required by the HIPAA Security Rule are kept for 6 years from the date they were created or last in effect, in line with 45 CFR 164.316, and longer if another rule applies.

If a record is lost, destroyed or accessed without authorization, the staff member reports it to the Privacy Officer the same day. The agency reconstructs the record where possible and handles the event under CR-03 and, where applicable, ENV-09.

If [AGENCY NAME] closes or ceases operation, the Administrator prepares a written closure plan. It notifies OHCQ and other regulators and payers as required, notifies each active client or representative in writing, and returns records to the client or representative on request or retains them as required for the periods in this policy. The plan names the person who will keep and secure the records and allow access, with that custodian's address ([ADDRESS]) and phone ([PHONE]) given to clients.

The Administrator reviews a sample of open and closed records at least quarterly for completeness, timeliness (including the 30-day discharge completion) and security. Results go to the QA committee (ADM-08), and corrective action is assigned and tracked.

policies.title: Required Reports to the State
policies.applies_to: Administrator, Director of Nursing/RN Supervisor, Billing and Compliance Staff, Office Staff, Owners and Governing Authority
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] files every report, survey, notice and response that Maryland requires of a Residential Service Agency (RSA) and Medicaid personal assistance provider, on time, accurately and with a retained record. These filings go to the Office of Health Care Quality (OHCQ), the Maryland Department of Health (MDH) and its Office of Long Term Services and Supports (OLTSS), the Division of Provider Integrity, Claims and Compliance (DPICC), the local department of social services, and the Maryland Department of Labor.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will meet all state reporting deadlines. The Administrator, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], is responsible for the reporting calendar. Every report is prepared from agency records, reviewed by a second person before submission, and filed with proof of submission. The agency reports as follows. (1) Incidents and complaints involving Medicaid participants are reported to the Department within 24 hours of the agency's knowledge, with a written report on the Department's form within 7 calendar days (COMAR 10.09.84.05). (2) Suspected abuse, neglect, self-neglect or exploitation is reported immediately to the local department of social services (COMAR 10.09.84.05). (3) At license renewal, the agency submits the annual OHCQ data collection survey with the renewal application, the renewal fee, substantively changed policies and current employee licenses and certificates (COMAR 10.07.05.04). (4) The agency files the annual HCBS Cost Survey by December 31, 2026. The Department will suspend payment from January 1, 2027 for non-filers (PT 16-27). (5) The agency files the annual personal care aide wage report with the Maryland Department of Labor by September 1 each year (HB 189/SB 371 of 2024, referenced in C29). (6) The agency gives 45 days' notice of a change in ownership, location, name or tax ID. (7) The agency answers any DPICC audit or plan-of-correction request within 15 calendar days, and responds to every outreach attempt (PT 13-27). The agency also tracks federal payment-adequacy and rate-transparency requirements (42 CFR 441.302(k); 42 CFR 447.203), including the direct-care compensation standard that MDH reports will apply from July 9, 2030. No report is delayed because the facts are incomplete; the agency files what it knows on time and supplements it later. Anyone who in good faith reports an incident, complaint or concern will not be retaliated against.

definitions.definition: The Maryland Department of Health, Office of Health Care Quality. It licenses RSAs under COMAR 10.07.05 and investigates complaints. Main phone is 410-402-8040, and the complaint line is 800-492-6005.

The Division of Provider Integrity, Claims and Compliance. It audits RSAs, issues plans of correction and may withhold payment.

An event or complaint involving a Medicaid participant that the Department requires to be reported within 24 hours of the agency's knowledge. Examples include injury, abuse, neglect, exploitation, a serious change in condition and a client complaint about services. See ENV-09 and CR-02.
The annual Home and Community-Based Services Cost Survey that Medicaid personal assistance providers must file with MDH. The agency's filing deadline for 2026 is December 31, 2026.
The annual personal care aide wage report that RSAs file with the Maryland Department of Labor by September 1.
The agency's written response to deficiencies found by OHCQ or DPICC, stating what will be corrected, by whom and by when.

procedures: The Administrator keeps a Required Reports Calendar listing every recurring and event-driven filing in this policy, with the due date, the responsible person, a backup person and the submission method. The calendar is reviewed at the start of each month and at the quarterly QA meeting (ADM-08).

Incident and complaint reports (24 hours): Any employee who learns of a reportable incident or complaint involving a Medicaid participant tells the RN Supervisor and Administrator immediately by phone, and in all cases the same day. The agency's 24-hour clock starts when any agency employee first knows of the event.

The Administrator or designee makes the initial report to the Department within 24 hours of the agency's knowledge, using the channel the Department specifies. The person making the report records the date, time, method, person contacted and the facts given on the incident log (ENV-09).

The RN Supervisor completes the written report on the Department's form within 7 calendar days of the agency's knowledge. The Administrator reviews it, signs it and submits it. A copy and proof of submission are filed in the incident file and the client record.
If a client's safety is at risk, staff first call 911 or arrange emergency care. The reporting steps then follow immediately and are not a reason to delay care (PC-09).

Suspected abuse, neglect, self-neglect or exploitation: Any employee who suspects it reports it right away to the local department of social services for the client's county, and then informs the Administrator. Employees do not wait for the Administrator's approval and do not investigate before reporting. The Administrator also files the 24-hour and 7-day Medicaid report where the client is a Medicaid participant. The agency follows ENV-08.

Complaints: Complaints are logged and handled under CR-02. Complaints from Medicaid participants are also reported to the Department within 24 hours of knowledge, with the written report in 7 calendar days. The agency tells clients they may also contact OHCQ's complaint line at 800-492-6005. The agency does not discourage or retaliate against anyone who contacts OHCQ.

Annual OHCQ data collection survey and license renewal: At least 120 days before the license expires, the Administrator opens a renewal file. The file includes the annual data collection survey, the $1,000 renewal fee, policies that have changed substantively (such as complaint handling and client evaluation), and valid licenses and certificates for all current employees. The agency submits the package to OHCQ well ahead of the expiration date and keeps proof of submission (ADM-11). A license is valid for 3 years.

HCBS Cost Survey: The Billing and Compliance Staff gather the required financial and cost data from payroll and accounting records no later than October 31. The Administrator reviews the survey for accuracy and files it before December 31, 2026. For later years the agency files by the deadline MDH sets. The confirmation is saved. The agency treats failure to file as a payment risk, because payment is suspended from January 1, 2027 for non-filers (PT 16-27).

Annual PCA wage report: By August 1 each year, Billing and Compliance Staff compile the personal care aide wage data from payroll for the reporting period. The Administrator reviews it against payroll and the wage floors in PER-08 and submits it to the Maryland Department of Labor by September 1. The confirmation is saved.

Payment-adequacy and rate transparency: The Administrator tracks MDH notices on the federal direct-care compensation standard, which MDH reports will apply from July 9, 2030, and on rate transparency requirements. Any change in required reporting is added to the calendar and to the cost and payroll reporting process (ADM-13).

Changes in ownership, location, name or tax ID: The Administrator gives written notice to OHCQ and updates Medicaid enrollment through MPRIME at least 45 days before the effective date. If a change is unforeseeable, notice is given as soon as the agency learns of it, and the reason is documented. The agency does not operate under a new owner, address, name or tax ID until the state has accepted the change (ADM-11).

DPICC audits and plans of correction: When a DPICC or OHCQ request or audit notice arrives, the person receiving it gives it to the Administrator the same day. The Administrator logs the date received and responds to every outreach attempt. The agency responds to any plan of correction within 15 calendar days. Records are produced completely and on time. The agency understands that non-responders are suspended after three outreach attempts (PT 13-27).

Repeat findings: The Administrator tracks every finding and its correction. If a finding repeats within 6 months, the Administrator briefs the owners the same week, because sanctions under COMAR 10.09.36 are possible. The root cause and corrective action are reviewed under ADM-08.

Cooperation with inspections and audits: Staff give OHCQ, OLTSS, DPICC and other authorized reviewers prompt access to records and clients as required (COMAR 10.09.84.05). The Administrator or designee escorts reviewers and keeps a log of what was requested and provided.

Accuracy and review: A second person verifies each report against source records before submission. Employees do not backdate, alter or omit facts. Corrections to a filed report are made by a signed, dated supplement.

Retention: Copies of every report, survey, notice, confirmation and related correspondence are kept in the compliance file. Records that support service documentation, including dates and hours, are retained 6 years from the date of service (COMAR 10.09.84.05) (REC-01).

Annual review: Each January the Administrator reviews the Required Reports Calendar against the current COMAR, MDH transmittals and OHCQ instructions, updates this policy and reports missed or late filings to the governing authority (ADM-01).

official.notes: OHCQ publishes no separate policy checklist for RSAs. The policy requirements are the 'Policies and Procedures' grid in the RSA License Application (pp.4-6) and COMAR 10.07.05.08B, which the application cites. The application also requires a business plan (including a description of agency services), an organizational chart, an SDAT letter of good standing and workers' compensation proof. These are not policy content and are excluded here. How the reviewer expects submission: (1) Submit a typed application, with the policies and the other attachments, through the OHCQ 'Submit a License Application' link. The application says handwritten applications are returned, and that there is no application fee. (2) Submit the policies as attachments. In each grid box, list the name of the attached document and the page numbers where that policy appears. Organize the manual under the five headings above, in the same order. This makes it easy to cross-reference every B(1) item. (3) To request a waiver of any item, list the policy in the waiver box and explain why it is inappropriate or unnecessary for this RSA. Then enter N/A in that item's box. This follows COMAR 10.07.05.08B(2). (4) Agencies that provide invasive equipment or supplies must arrange 24-hour-a-day equipment maintenance service (COMAR 10.07.05.08B(3)). The application asks about this as a yes/no question. (5) The RSA Certification on worker classification of personal care aides is a separate online form under Health-General §19-4A-11. All applicants must complete it, including those that will not hire personal care aides. (6) Branch offices use the parent's policies. Adding a new home health care service later requires the full application again, with policies for the new service. (7) At renewal, submit any policies that changed substantively, including those on complaint handling and client evaluation and assessment (COMAR 10.07.05.04I(3)). (8) Limits of this result: the grid is built around home health care services, so a non-medical RSA may request waivers for items such as drug administration and enteral/parenteral nutrition. The application does not list COMAR's other chapter requirements, such as the complaint process (.09), screening (.10) and training (.11), as grid items, and I did not fetch those sections. I also did not review the Medicaid program rules (COMAR 10.09.84 and 10.09.20) for additional written-policy requirements.
